There is a law in Leviticus so strange that most Christians have never heard it preached, and the ones who have heard of it have been taught to file it under abolished. Every fiftieth year, a trumpet sounds on the Day of Atonement, and the whole economy resets. Land sold returns to the family that lost it. Debts dissolve. Those who sold themselves into servitude to survive a bad harvest walk free. The God of Israel built into the calendar a planned and recurring undoing of accumulation. He called it Jubilee. And the church has spent two millennia finding reasons He could not have been serious.

The question underneath the question is whether Jubilee is a spiritualized antique, a poetic foreshadowing of the soul's release in Christ and nothing more, or whether it is what it plainly claims to be, an economic command with teeth, a structural mercy God legislated into the bone of a society. If it is only a metaphor, we can admire it. If it is a command, it indicts us.

The spine runs through the text itself. You shall consecrate the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee for you, when each of you shall return to his property and each of you shall return to his clan (Leviticus 25:10 ESV). The word for liberty is deror, the same word that turns up centuries later when Isaiah's anointed one proclaims liberty to the captives, the same passage Jesus reads in the synagogue at Nazareth and then sits down and says this is fulfilled today. Hold that thread. It runs from the auction block of an Israelite farmer all the way to the carpenter standing up in His hometown, and it is the same word, the same release, the same economy.

Let me give the strongest case for the dismissal, because serious people make it and they are not lazy. The argument runs like this. There is little hard evidence that Israel ever actually practiced the Jubilee on a national scale. The rabbis themselves debated whether it applied once the tribes were scattered. It belongs to a vanished agrarian world of clan land tenure that has no analog in a modern credit economy. To drag it into the present is to commit a category error, to mistake ancient Near Eastern legislation for a policy proposal. And the New Testament, the objection continues, takes the language of Jubilee and fills it with spiritual content. Jesus proclaims release from the captivity of sin, not a literal land redistribution. The release was always pointing past itself to the soul. To literalize it is to miss the gospel for the economics.

I want to grant what is true here, and a good deal is. Jubilee does point past itself. Jesus does fill deror with a depth no land transfer could hold. The captivity He breaks is older and deeper than debt. And it is genuinely true that we cannot lift bronze-age agrarian statutes and drop them unmodified into a world of mortgages and sovereign bonds. Anyone who reads Leviticus 25 as a ready-made fiscal bill has not understood Leviticus or fiscal policy. So the objection's caution is earned. Jubilee is not a spreadsheet.

But watch what the dismissal quietly does. It takes the fact that Jubilee points beyond economics and converts it into the claim that Jubilee was never about economics at all. That move is not exegesis. It is evasion dressed as exegesis. Because the text could not be more concrete. It is not talking about the soul. It is talking about fields, in cubits, with a formula. Leviticus even regulates the sale price, telling buyers to count the years until the next Jubilee and price the land accordingly, because what you are really buying is a number of harvests, not the ground itself (Leviticus 25:15-16 ESV). You cannot spiritualize a pricing formula. God is doing economics here, deliberately, in detail, and the detail is the point.

And the reason for the detail is given in one sentence that breaks the whole modern theory of property. The land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me (Leviticus 25:23 ESV). There it is. The reason debts release and land returns is that no Israelite ever owned the land in the first place. God owned it. They were tenants, resident aliens on ground that was His, holding it in trust. Jubilee is not charity from owner to owner. It is the landlord reminding His tenants that the deeds they have been trading were never absolute. Property, in the economy God commanded, is real but penultimate. It is held, not possessed. That single conviction, that ultimate ownership belongs to God and human ownership is stewardship under Him, is the foundation the dismissal has to bury in order to keep Jubilee safely in the past.

The history of debt explains why we want it buried. Gary Anderson has shown how deeply the grammar of debt runs through the biblical imagination, how sin itself came to be pictured as an obligation recorded against the sinner, a weight that must be paid down or forgiven (Anderson 2009). The two languages, financial debt and moral debt, were never separate in the Hebrew mind. Which is why the release of one was always a sign of the release of the other. When Israel forgave a neighbor's loan, it was rehearsing in coin what it hoped God would do in mercy. Ched Myers has argued that this Sabbath-Jubilee tradition forms a connected economic vision running from the manna in the wilderness, where those who gathered much had nothing left over, straight through to the early Jerusalem church holding all things in common (Myers 2001). The thread is not incidental. It is Scripture's quarrel with accumulation, sustained across a thousand years.

And the church kept the quarrel alive longer than we remember. For over a thousand years it forbade usury, the lending of money at interest, on the ground that money is barren and to charge for time is to sell what belongs to God alone, since time is not yours to sell. That prohibition held from the early councils through the medieval schoolmen until the pressures of early modern commerce finally cracked it in the sixteenth century. The crack did not come because someone disproved the theology. It came because the money was too good to refuse. We did not refute the doctrine of Jubilee. We outgrew our willingness to be bound by it.

Then the reversal. The dismissal says Jubilee is impractical, that no real economy could absorb a periodic cancellation of debt without collapse. But turn the objection over. The reason a modern economy could not survive a Jubilee is precisely the reason Israel needed one. Our system runs on permanent, compounding, inescapable debt as its operating principle. We have built a machine that requires that the farmer never get his land back, that the obligation never be released, that the poor man's bad year follow him into his children's lives and his children's children's. When we say Jubilee is unrealistic, we are not making an argument against Jubilee. We are confessing exactly the bondage Jubilee was given to break. The impracticality is the diagnosis. The objection, spoken honestly, is the symptom of the disease.

This is where the cross does its work, and it does it as law before grace. The law of Jubilee says that without periodic release, an economy will grind the poor into permanent servitude, and that no one inside it stays clean, because the man who holds the note benefits from the bondage even while he tells himself he is merely being prudent. I hold notes. I have lent and expected return. The law indicts the lender in me. Then grace. Jesus stands in Nazareth, reads the Jubilee promise of release, and announces that the trumpet has sounded in His own body. He is the Jubilee Israel never fully kept. On the cross He pays the debt that the Day of Atonement only pictured, and the deror, the liberty, breaks loose at last, not as a metaphor that replaces the economics but as the depth the economics was always reaching toward. The release of the captives and the release of the debtor were never two things. They were the same mercy at two depths.

So what do we do with a law God commanded and we have spent two thousand years explaining away. We do not pretend we can legislate Leviticus 25 into a modern budget unaltered. That much the objection won. But neither do we get to keep the comfortable lie that because it points to Christ it asks nothing of our checkbooks. The God who said the land is mine has not changed His mind about who owns what. We are still strangers and sojourners with Him, holding deeds that were never absolute, on ground that was never finally ours. Jubilee asks whether we will live as if that is true, whether we will forgive a debt we are owed, return what we have accumulated, loosen our grip on the field while we still can.

The trumpet sounded on the Day of Atonement, when the nation's sins were carried away. That is not an accident of the calendar. God set the release of debts on the same day He set the release of guilt, because in His economy they were always the same act. We have learned to want the second and refuse the first. The God who commanded both is still waiting to see if we believed Him.

### Works Cited

Anderson, Gary A. Sin: A History. New Haven: Yale University Press, 2009.

Myers, Ched. The Biblical Vision of Sabbath Economics. Washington, DC: Tell the Word, 2001.

Wright, Christopher J. H. Old Testament Ethics for the People of God. Downers Grove: InterVarsity Press, 2004.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

chapters.title: Lament: The Prayer the Church Forgot
chapters.summary: We taught ourselves to skip past the prayers of grief, and in skipping them we lost the only language honest enough to carry what race has done.
chapters.body:
Open the hymnal of most white churches and try to find a song that does not resolve. Try to find one that ends in the question and not the answer, that leaves the grief standing, that does not hurry to the bridge where everything is fine. You will be looking a long time. We have a thousand songs of triumph and almost none of sorrow, and that absence is not a matter of taste. It is a theology, and it has cost us the ability to speak honestly about race.

A full third of the Psalms are laments, prayers of complaint, grief, and protest addressed to God. They are not polite. How long, O Lord. Will you forget me forever (Psalm 13:1 ESV). My God, my God, why have you forsaken me (Psalm 22:1 ESV). These are not the prayers of people whose faith is failing. They are the prayers of the most faithful people in the Bible, and Jesus himself died with one of them on his lips. Lament is not the opposite of faith. It is faith refusing to lie about the state of the world.

Let me carry one psalm as the spine. Psalm 13 moves in three movements, and the church has learned to live only in the last. It opens in complaint, four times the cry how long, the prayer of a man who feels forgotten by the God he still addresses. Then it turns to petition, consider and answer me, light up my eyes. And only at the end does it arrive at trust, I will sing to the Lord because he has dealt bountifully with me (Psalm 13:6 ESV). Three movements. Complaint, petition, trust. We skip the first two and sing only the third, and a third of a prayer is not a prayer. It is a performance of arrival we have not actually made.

Now the strong objection, because there is one. Some will say that lament risks becoming a wallow, that endless grief over race keeps wounds open that grace means to close, that the gospel calls us to rejoice and to forgive and to look forward, not to camp in lamentation as if the resurrection had not happened. They say a faith fixated on sorrow has forgotten the empty tomb. And there is truth here worth holding. The Christian does not grieve as one without hope. Lament that never moves toward trust curdles into despair, and despair is not a Christian word.

But notice what the objection assumes. It assumes that the choice is between grief and hope, when the Psalms refuse that choice entirely. Psalm 13 does not arrive at trust by skipping the complaint. It arrives at trust through the complaint, by way of it, having spoken the grief fully to God first. The hope at the end of the psalm is earned, weighted, real, precisely because the sorrow at the beginning was not censored. A church that cannot lament cannot truly hope either, because its hope has never passed through honesty. It has only passed around it. And a hope that goes around the wound is a denial wearing the mask of faith.

Here is where this touches race directly. The reason the white church struggles to speak about race is, in part, a liturgical failure. We have no language for it. We know how to celebrate and we know how to instruct, but we do not know how to grieve, because we deleted grief from our worship generations ago. So when the history of slavery and lynching and segregation is set before us, we have no vessel to receive it. We reach for explanation, for defense, for the quick turn to reconciliation, because we never learned the prayer that simply sits in the wreckage and says to God, how long. The Black church kept that prayer. The spirituals were lament, the slave singing nobody knows the trouble I have seen straight into the face of God. We who lost lament lost the very language the moment required.

The history is specific and the silence around it is the proof. From 1877 to 1950 the historians at the Equal Justice Initiative have documented more than four thousand racial terror lynchings in the American South, public killings often attended by churchgoing crowds, sometimes on a Sunday, sometimes with the body displayed near a house of worship. The white church of that era did not lament these murders. It largely watched, or looked away, or in some cases supplied the crowd. There is no widely sung hymn of grief for them. The absence of that lament, eighty years on, is itself a sin we have not confessed. We never even learned to cry about it.

Walter Brueggemann argues that the loss of lament is the loss of a whole dimension of faith, that a community which can only praise has surrendered its capacity to hold God accountable and to tell the truth about its own pain (Brueggemann 1986). Without lament, he says, the covenant becomes one-sided, a relationship in which the powerful are never questioned and the suffering are never heard. A church that cannot lament cannot do justice, because justice begins with the truthful naming of what is wrong, and that naming, addressed to God, is exactly what lament is. We traded the prayer for a smile, and we lost the truth in the trade.

Here is the reversal. We have treated lament as a sign of weak faith, a stage to grow out of, a sorrow that mature believers transcend. But the Bible treats lament as a sign of intimacy. You do not complain to a stranger. You complain to a father, to the one you trust enough to be honest with, to the one you believe is listening and able. The freedom to cry how long, O Lord is the freedom of a child who knows the father is there. To refuse lament is not strength. It is distance. It is a politeness that has stopped believing God can take the truth.

The cross does the deepest work here, and it does it before it comforts. On the cross Jesus prayed Psalm 22, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me, and in praying it he sanctified lament forever. God himself, in the flesh, lamented. The sinless one took the prayer of grief onto his own lips and made it holy. So there is no spiritual height above lament, because the highest one stooped into it. The law here is plain. A church too proud to grieve is a church that thinks itself above its own Lord.

And the grace is this. Because Christ lamented and was heard, our laments are heard too. The how long is not a cry into an empty sky. It rises to a God who has himself cried it, who knows the weight of the forsaken from the inside, who will not despise the broken prayer because he prayed it first. We are free to grieve all the way down, because the bottom is not despair. The bottom is a man on a cross who got there before us.

We forgot how to lament, and forgetting it, we lost the only honest language we had for what race has done. The first repentance may be smaller and harder than we think. Not a program. A prayer. How long, O Lord. We have not even begun to pray it.

### Works Cited

Brueggemann, Walter. The Costly Loss of Lament. Journal for the Study of the Old Testament 36 (1986): 57-71.

Equal Justice Initiative. Lynching in America: Confronting the Legacy of Racial Terror. Montgomery: Equal Justice Initiative, 2017.

Thurman, Howard. Jesus and the Disinherited. Boston: Beacon Press, 1949.

chapters.title: Mental Health and the Church: Beyond Just Pray About It
chapters.summary: A church that treats depression as a faith problem will keep handing the drowning a heavier stone.
chapters.body:
A woman sat across from me in my office and told me she had stopped wanting to be alive. She had told her small group the week before and been advised to pray more and trust God. She had been praying. She had been trusting God for eleven years through a depression that the praying had not lifted, and the advice had landed on her not as comfort but as verdict, one more proof that her suffering was a measure of her failing faith. She left that group. She nearly left the church. She nearly left more than that. I have replayed that conversation many times, because the counsel she received was not malicious. It was sincere, and it was lethal, and some version of it has come out of my own mouth.

The real question is not whether Christians should care about mental health. Of course they should, and most will say so. The real question is what the church believes mental suffering is. Underneath the counsel to 'just pray about it' lies a theology, usually unexamined, that the mind is the seat of the spirit and that a sick mind is therefore a sick soul. Get that theology wrong and every kind word becomes an accusation. The depressed hear that their condition is a sin to repent of. The anxious hear that their fear is a failure to believe. We hand the drowning a heavier stone and call it encouragement.

The strongest form of the objection is worth stating fairly, because it is not pure ignorance and it guards something true. It runs this way. The Bible promises peace that surpasses understanding. It commands us not to be anxious. It says the joy of the Lord is our strength. To rush a suffering believer to a psychiatrist, the concern goes, is to treat as medical what is finally spiritual, to medicate away a soul's true ache, to let the culture redefine sin as illness and conviction as a chemical imbalance. There is a real danger there. Our age does sometimes flatten the moral into the clinical, calling a thing a disorder so no one has to call it anything harder. A church that simply outsourced every inner struggle to medication would have abandoned its calling. That much is right.

But the strong objection collapses on a single body, and the body is the prophet Elijah. Carry his story as the spine, because Scripture refuses to spiritualize him. In 1 Kings 19, immediately after the greatest victory of his ministry on Mount Carmel, Elijah runs into the wilderness, sits under a broom tree, and prays to die. 'It is enough,' he says, 'now, O Lord, take away my life' (1 Kings 19:4 ESV). Here is a man of titanic faith, fresh off calling down fire from heaven, in the grip of what any honest reader recognizes as suicidal despair. Now watch what God does, because it is the whole sermon. God does not rebuke him. God does not tell him to pray more or trust harder or claim a promise. God lets him sleep. Then an angel wakes him and feeds him. Then lets him sleep again, and feeds him again. 'And he lay down and slept under a broom tree. And behold, an angel touched him and said to him, Arise and eat' (1 Kings 19:5 ESV). Before a single word of theology, God addresses Elijah's body. Rest. Food. Then more rest, more food. Only after the body is tended does the quiet voice come, and even then it does not scold. The divine response to a faithful man's collapse is not a lecture. It is sleep and bread.

This is the text the church has skipped. We have read Elijah as a hero and refused to read him as a sufferer, because a depressed prophet complicates a theology that needs faith and despair to be opposites. They are not. Curt Thompson, a psychiatrist who works at the intersection of faith and the brain, names the mechanism the church most often ignores. Shame. Shame works by isolation, he argues, driving us into hiding precisely from the community and vulnerability that would heal it, the very things we need most (Thompson 2015). The suffering believer who is told her depression is a faith deficiency is driven into hiding by shame, away from the one community that might hold her, deeper into the isolation that feeds the illness. The very counsel meant to help operates the engine that destroys. Elijah's God did the opposite. He came to Elijah in his hiding place and fed him there.

Trace the history and the wound is partly our own making. For most of Christian history the care of the soul and the care of the mind were not split. The monastic tradition knew acedia, the noonday demon, a paralyzing heaviness the desert fathers treated with rhythm, labor, and community, not condemnation. Then came the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, the rise of modern medicine, and a hard fork. The body and mind went to the doctors. The soul went to the clergy. Each side guarded its territory and grew suspicious of the other, and the church, having ceded the brain to medicine, was left preaching to a self it no longer believed was embodied. By the twentieth century much of American evangelicalism treated psychology as a rival gospel, antidepressants as a crutch for the faithless, the counselor's office as a place real Christians did not need. We built that wall. I was handed it already built and I reinforced it before I knew what it was.

Here the reversal the gospel always brings. We assume strong faith means the absence of anguish, that the mature believer has moved past the dark places. Scripture gives us a Savior in a garden, sweating, begging, asking that the cup pass, 'sorrowful, even to death' (Matthew 26:38 ESV). The most faithful human being who ever lived experienced anguish so severe that Luke, a physician, records his sweat falling like drops of blood. Mental and emotional torment is not the opposite of faith. It sat in the soul of the Son of God on the worst night of human history. The presence of anguish proves nothing about the absence of faith. The garden settles that forever.

And the cross does the deepest work, against the lie underneath all the bad counsel. The lie is that suffering this severe must be punishment, that the depressed are reaping what their weak faith has sown, that affliction is the wage of some hidden sin. The cross detonates that arithmetic. There the only truly innocent man bore the most extreme anguish, body and mind and spirit, and bore it precisely because suffering is not a clean ledger of personal fault. Kelly Kapic writes that the cross frees us from the cruelty of believing our pain is always our own doing (Kapic 2017). Christ cried out that he was forsaken. If forsakenness can pass through the soul of the sinless one, then the darkness in the soul of a suffering saint is not the proof of God's absence. It may be the very place he is nearest, with bread, the way he came to Elijah.

The woman in my office did not need a heavier stone. She needed what the angel brought the prophet under the broom tree. Rest. Food. A presence that did not flinch from her despair or assign it a moral grade. She needed the church to stop preaching at her drowning and to get in the water. We have the resources for this, the medicine and the counselors and the doctors God has given, and we have the deeper resource, a God who feeds the despairing before he teaches them.

Pray about it. Yes. And then bring the bread.

### Works Cited

Kapic, Kelly M. Embodied Hope: A Theological Meditation on Pain and Suffering. Downers Grove: IVP Academic, 2017.

Thompson, Curt. The Soul of Shame: Retelling the Stories We Believe About Ourselves. Downers Grove: IVP Books, 2015.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

chapters.title: Principalities and Powers: The Bible's Language for Systems
chapters.summary: Paul had a vocabulary for systemic evil two thousand years before the word systemic existed.
chapters.body:
There is a phrase in Paul that the modern reader hurries past, because it sounds like superstition, like something we have outgrown. 'For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places' (Ephesians 6:12 ESV). Rulers, authorities, powers, forces. We read it and picture demons with horns, and either we believe in those or we do not, and either way we file the verse under a worldview we no longer share. But what if Paul is not talking about the thing we think he is talking about. What if Paul, in the first century, had a precise vocabulary for exactly the thing we now call systemic evil, and we have been too modern to hear it.

The real question under this essay is whether the Bible has any language for systems at all, or whether systemic talk is a recent import smuggled into Scripture by people with a political agenda. That is a fair challenge and I want to take it seriously. Plenty of thoughtful Christians suspect that the whole discourse of systemic sin is a modern sociological frame laid over a book that only ever talks about individual hearts. If that suspicion is right, then much of what I have been writing is sand. So everything turns on this. Did the biblical writers themselves have a category for the evil that is bigger than any individual.

Let me steel-man the skeptic, because the skeptic is guarding something real. The worry is that talk of principalities and powers as systems is a sleight of hand, a way to make Paul endorse a modern political program by spiritualizing institutions he never had in mind. Paul, the skeptic says, believed in literal spiritual beings, fallen angels, dark intelligences, and to convert those into a metaphor for capitalism or racism or any structure you happen to dislike is to use the apostle as a ventriloquist's dummy. Worse, it risks letting individuals escape responsibility by blaming invisible forces, the devil made the system do it. This worry is protecting the integrity of the text against our endless temptation to make it say whatever our moment wants, and it is protecting personal accountability against a cosmic alibi. It deserves an answer, not a dismissal.

Here is the answer, and it comes from the language itself. The Greek words Paul uses, the archai and exousiai and dunameis, rulers and authorities and powers, were not exotic demon names. They were ordinary words for ordinary structures. Exousia is the word for institutional authority, the kind a magistrate holds, the kind Rome conferred. Arche means a ruling office, a principality in the political sense, a beginning point of power. Paul uses this same vocabulary in Romans 13 for the governing authorities you pay taxes to. These words straddle the visible and the invisible on purpose. Walter Wink spent three volumes demonstrating that for Paul the powers are always both at once, an outer, visible, institutional form and an inner, invisible spirituality, the animating drive of the institution (Wink 1984). The power is not the demon instead of the system, and it is not the system instead of the demon. It is the system together with the spirit that drives it. Paul refuses our either or. He sees a corporation, an empire, a market, a temple establishment, as having a visible body of policies and personnel and an invisible interiority that outlives any individual inside it and bends them all toward its ends.

This is why the skeptic's fear of a cosmic alibi misfires. Paul's language does the opposite of excusing the individual. It explains why the individual cannot fight the harm alone, because the harm is not located in any single individual. When Wink described the powers, he showed that an institution can have a spirit that is genuinely evil even when every person inside it is, individually, just doing his job (Wink 1984). The power is the emergent thing, the way the whole behaves as if it had a will, a momentum no one person authored and no one person can stop. That is not an alibi. That is a diagnosis of why so much evil persists with no villain you can point to. The principalities are Paul's word for precisely the phenomenon we struggle to name, the evil that is real and structural and bigger than the sum of the people who serve it.

The text I want to carry is from Colossians, and it does the decisive work. Paul writes of Christ that 'by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities, all things were created through him and for him' (Colossians 1:16 ESV). Read that carefully, because it changes everything. The powers were created. They are not originally evil. Thrones, dominions, rulers, authorities, the structures of ordered human life, were made through Christ and for Christ. Government, economy, family, law, culture, these are part of the good creation, the framework within which shalom is meant to be woven (Plantinga 1995). The systems are not the enemy by nature. They are creatures. Which means the skeptic is right that we must not simply demonize every institution, and also that the structures are real enough to be named as creatures with a vocation.

But creatures fall. The same powers that were created good have rebelled, have absolutized themselves, have demanded the loyalty owed only to God and turned from servants of human flourishing into devourers of it. This is the biblical account of systemic evil, and it is neither naive nor cynical. The system is not innocent machinery, and it is not irredeemable darkness. It is a good creation in revolt, a fallen power, an institution that has made itself a god. Augustine described the earthly city as built by the libido dominandi, the lust to dominate organized into a whole civilization, good order corrupted into an engine of self glory (Augustine 426). That is a fallen power. Niebuhr described the nation as a community that demands ultimate devotion and commits in its corporate life the very sins it forbids its individual members, a structure that becomes idolatrous precisely by becoming powerful (Niebuhr 1932). That too is a fallen power. Paul gave us the word two thousand years before our word existed.

The reversal is that I have served fallen powers while imagining myself free. I belong to institutions, a denomination, a nation, an economy, and I have given them a loyalty I told myself was merely practical, while they shaped my desires and bounded my imagination and decided in advance which questions I was allowed to ask. I did not choose the spirit of the systems I inhabit. I absorbed it, the way a fish does not choose the water. The principalities do not announce themselves. They feel like common sense, like the way things simply are, and that invisibility is their power over me. I have been more discipled by the powers than I would ever admit from a pulpit, and the first work of the prophetic word is to make the water visible.

Now the cross, where the powers meet their judgment, and this is the line the whole essay has been moving toward. Paul finishes the thought in Colossians. Christ 'disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him' (Colossians 2:15 ESV). The same powers, the archai and exousiai, are disarmed at the cross. Here is how. The powers rule by the threat of death. They keep us in line by fear, fear of cost, exclusion, suffering, the fear Stringfellow named as the chain the powers use to bind us, the fear that makes good people serve bad systems rather than pay the price of resistance (Stringfellow 1973). At Golgotha the powers, Rome and the temple establishment together, used their ultimate weapon. They killed God. And he rose. The weapon was spent and the wielder was empty handed. Death, the powers' final threat, was shown to be a defeated thing, which means the fear is broken, which means a person freed by the resurrection can finally stop serving the system out of dread and start telling it the truth.

This is why the cross does real argumentative work and not just devotional comfort. It establishes that the powers are real, that the skeptic was wrong to reduce them to private sin, because you do not need to disarm a private sin, you repent of it. You disarm an army. Paul uses the language of a conquered enemy led in a victory procession, stripped, shamed, paraded. The cross treats systemic evil as a defeated combatant, which means systemic evil was a combatant. And the cross establishes that the powers are not ultimate, that they are creatures who fell and creatures who can be put in their place, which guards against the despair that says the system is god and resistance is futile. Oliver O'Donovan argued that the resurrection reestablishes the authority of the true order over the pretended autonomy of the powers, so that Christian engagement with systems is neither worship nor war without hope but the confident reassertion of a kingdom that has already won the decisive battle (O'Donovan 1986).

So the law comes first. The powers are real, they are fallen, they have discipled you, and you have served them while calling it common sense. That is the diagnosis and it should unsettle the part of us that thinks we stand outside any system, pure and uncaptured. None of us does. Then grace. The same cross that names the powers has disarmed them, broken the fear that was their leash, and freed the captured to resist what they once could only obey.

Paul was not being superstitious. He was being precise. He saw the thing we are still struggling to see, the evil that wears an institution like a body and outlives every person who serves it. He named it, he traced it to a good creation in revolt, and he announced its defeat at a Roman execution that the powers themselves arranged, not knowing they were signing their own surrender. We do not wrestle against flesh and blood. We never only did. And the One we follow has already stripped the enemy we are still afraid of.

Plantinga, Cornelius. 1995. Not the Way It's Supposed to Be: A Breviary of Sin. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Stringfellow, William. 1973. An Ethic for Christians and Other Aliens in a Strange Land. Waco: Word Books.

Wink, Walter. 1984. Naming the Powers: The Language of Power in the New Testament. Philadelphia: Fortress Press.

chapters.title: The Black Church: The Most Important Institution in American Christianity
chapters.summary: The Black church did not emerge as a branch of American Protestantism. It emerged in spite of it. Born in the crucible of enslavement, sustained through Jim Crow, and central to the most significant moral movement in American history, the Black church is the tradition white Christianity has never adequately reckoned with.
chapters.body:
There is no single institution in American history that has done more with fewer resources, under greater oppression, with less recognition, than the Black church. It educated a people when education was illegal. It organized a community when organization was punishable by death. It produced a theology of liberation a century before European theologians gave it a name. And it did all of this while white Christianity, with rare exceptions, either ignored it, opposed it, or patronized it.

To understand the Black church is to understand that it was never merely a religious institution. It was the school, the bank, the political caucus, the mutual aid society, the concert hall, and the courtroom of a people systematically excluded from every other institution in American life. The church was the one place where Black Americans could be fully human, fully vocal, and fully free. That this institution was built on a faith given to them by their enslavers, and then transformed into something their enslavers could not recognize, is one of the most remarkable feats of theological creativity in the history of Christianity.

The Invisible Institution

The religious life of enslaved Africans in America began in secrecy and subversion. Slaveholders had a complicated relationship with the Christianization of enslaved people. Some believed, or claimed to believe, that baptism conferred freedom, which made them reluctant to allow it. Others promoted a carefully controlled version of Christianity that emphasized obedience: "Slaves, obey your masters" (Ephesians 6:5) was the most frequently cited verse on the plantation. The Christianity offered to enslaved people was a theology of submission, designed to baptize the existing order and render resistance sinful.

The enslaved did not accept this theology. In what historian Albert Raboteau called "the invisible institution," enslaved people gathered in secret, in woods and hollows, in what came to be known as "hush arbors" or "brush arbors," spaces concealed from the surveillance of the slaveholder. There, beyond the reach of the master's Christianity, they developed their own theology, their own worship practices, and their own reading of Scripture.

And they read Scripture differently. Where the slaveholder saw Paul's injunction to obedience, the enslaved saw the Exodus. The God of the Bible was not the God of the plantation chapel, a deity who sanctioned hierarchy and demanded compliance. The God of the hush arbor was the God who heard the cry of the oppressed, who sent Moses to Pharaoh, who parted the sea, who brought down the mighty and lifted up the lowly. This was not an incidental difference in interpretation. It was a fundamentally different encounter with the text, born of a fundamentally different social location.

The Spirituals: Theology Encoded in Music

The spirituals were not merely songs. They were systematic theology set to music, encoded communication, and survival strategy rolled into one. When enslaved people sang "Go Down, Moses," they were not performing a quaint folk melody. They were articulating a theology of liberation: God intervenes in history on behalf of the oppressed. Pharaoh is not merely an ancient Egyptian ruler. Pharaoh is the slaveholder. Egypt is not merely a historical location. Egypt is the plantation. The promised land is not merely Canaan. The promised land is freedom.

"Wade in the Water" functioned simultaneously as worship and practical instruction: escaping enslaved people should walk through water to throw off the scent for tracking dogs. "Steal Away to Jesus" was both a hymn of spiritual longing and a signal that a secret meeting was being called. "Swing Low, Sweet Chariot" may have referenced the Underground Railroad. The genius of the spirituals was their double meaning: they could be sung openly because their surface meaning was pious, while their deeper meaning was revolutionary.

W.E.B. Du Bois recognized this in The Souls of Black Folk (1903), devoting his final chapter to "The Sorrow Songs." Du Bois heard in the spirituals "the singular spiritual heritage of the nation and the greatest gift of the Negro people," a music that carried the full weight of suffering, faith, resistance, and hope. The spirituals were the first original American contribution to world Christianity, and they came not from the seminaries of the powerful but from the fields of the enslaved.

Richard Allen and the Institutional Church

The transition from invisible institution to visible institution is embodied in the life of Richard Allen (1760-1831). Born enslaved in Philadelphia, Allen converted to Methodism, purchased his freedom, and became a licensed preacher. He worshipped at St. George's Methodist Episcopal Church in Philadelphia until 1787, when he and other Black congregants were physically pulled from their knees during prayer for sitting in seats that white members claimed. Allen walked out and never returned.

In 1794, Allen founded Bethel African Methodist Episcopal Church in Philadelphia. In 1816, he established the African Methodist Episcopal (AME) Church as an independent denomination, the first major religious denomination in the Western world founded by and for Black people. The AME Church was not merely a religious organization. It was a declaration of institutional independence, a refusal to accept spiritual equality in theory while enduring physical humiliation in practice.

Other denominations followed. The African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church was organized in 1821. Black Baptist churches, which had existed independently since the late eighteenth century, organized into state and national conventions throughout the nineteenth century, eventually forming the National Baptist Convention in 1895, which remains the largest African American religious organization in the United States. These institutions became the infrastructure of Black communal life in America.

The Center of Community Life

After Emancipation, the Black church became the primary institution around which freed Black communities organized themselves. In an America that systematically excluded Black people from political participation, economic opportunity, and educational access, the church filled every gap.

It was the school: Black churches established some of the earliest schools for freed people. Many historically Black colleges and universities, including Morehouse, Spelman, Fisk, and Howard, have roots in church-sponsored education. It was the bank: when formal financial institutions refused to serve Black communities, church-based mutual aid societies, burial societies, and lending circles provided economic infrastructure. It was the political forum: in a society where Black political expression was suppressed by violence, the church was the one institution where leadership could be developed, oratory could be practiced, and organizing could occur with some degree of safety. It was the cultural center: the Black church produced musicians, writers, artists, and intellectuals who shaped American culture far beyond the boundaries of the congregation.

The sociologist E. Franklin Frazier described the Black church as "a nation within a nation," and the phrase is not hyperbolic. For a people denied the full benefits of American citizenship, the church provided an alternative civic structure, complete with its own leaders, its own social services, its own educational system, and its own moral authority.

A Liberation Theology Before Liberation Theology

When Gustavo Gutierrez published A Theology of Liberation in 1971, launching the academic field of liberation theology, he was systematizing insights that the Black church had been practicing for two centuries. The enslaved did not need a European-educated Peruvian priest to tell them that God takes sides with the oppressed. They had read Exodus. They had sung the spirituals. They had built institutions of resistance and survival on the theological conviction that the God of Jesus Christ is not neutral in the face of injustice.

This theology was not written in academic treatises. It was preached from pulpits, sung in choirs, and lived in daily acts of resistance and mutual care. It was a theology of practice before it was a theology of theory. And it was profoundly orthodox in ways that its critics often failed to recognize. The Black church did not embrace liberation theology as a departure from traditional Christianity. It understood liberation as the meaning of traditional Christianity. The God who freed Israel from Egypt, who announced good news to the poor through Jesus, who raised the crucified one from the dead, was a God whose very nature was oriented toward the liberation of the oppressed.

The Civil Rights Movement as a Church Movement

The civil rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s was, at its core, a church movement. This fact has been so thoroughly secularized in popular memory that many Americans do not fully grasp it. Martin Luther King Jr. was not a political activist who happened to be a minister. He was a minister whose activism was an expression of his theology. His nonviolent philosophy was grounded in a synthesis of the Social Gospel, Gandhian nonviolence, and the Black church tradition of prophetic witness. His rhetoric was sermonic. His organizing structure was ecclesial. The Southern Christian Leadership Conference was a coalition of ministers. The mass meetings were worship services. The freedom songs were spirituals and hymns adapted for a new moment of liberation.

Fannie Lou Hamer, who helped organize the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party and challenged the segregationist delegation at the 1964 Democratic National Convention, was a church woman whose courage was rooted in her faith. When she testified before the credentials committee, she quoted Scripture. When she was beaten in a Winona, Mississippi, jail, she sang hymns. Her famous declaration, "I'm sick and tired of being sick and tired," was not secular frustration. It was prophetic lament.

John Lewis, who would serve in Congress for three decades, was trained in nonviolent resistance at workshops organized by the Nashville Christian Leadership Council. His concept of "good trouble" was theological before it was political. The willingness to absorb violence without retaliation, to suffer for justice, to love one's enemies, these were not merely strategic calculations. They were spiritual disciplines rooted in the cross.

The civil rights movement was the most successful moral revolution in American history, and it was led, organized, funded, and sustained by the Black church. No other institution, not the federal government, not the academy, not the media, played a comparable role. This is a fact that white American Christianity has never fully reckoned with: the most Christlike movement in American history was organized by the people white Christians had enslaved, segregated, and excluded.

Black Theology: James Cone and the God of the Oppressed

James Cone (1938-2018) gave academic form to what the Black church had always known. His 1969 book Black Theology and Black Power, followed by A Black Theology of Liberation (1970) and God of the Oppressed (1975), argued that theology must be done from the perspective of the oppressed, that the God of the Bible is unambiguously on the side of the marginalized, and that any theology that does not address the reality of racial oppression is not Christian theology at all.

Cone's work was deliberately provocative. He wrote that "Christ is Black" not as a statement about Jesus's physical appearance but as a theological claim: Christ identifies with the oppressed, and in America, the oppressed are disproportionately Black. He challenged white theology's pretension to universality, arguing that all theology is contextual and that white theology's failure to address racism was not neutrality but complicity.

White theologians were scandalized. Many dismissed Cone as a polemicist. But his central claim, that a theology that ignores the suffering of the oppressed is not faithful to the God of the Bible, is difficult to refute on scriptural grounds. The prophets of Israel, Jesus's inaugural sermon in Luke 4, the Magnificat of Mary, the parable of the sheep and the goats, all point toward a God whose concern for the marginalized is not incidental but definitional.

The Prosperity Gospel in Black Churches

The presence of the prosperity gospel in Black churches requires careful analysis that avoids both uncritical acceptance and condescending dismissal. When prosperity theology appears in a community that has been systematically denied economic opportunity for centuries, it carries a different meaning than when it appears in a white suburban megachurch.

For many Black prosperity preachers and their congregations, the message that God wants you to prosper is not merely about individual wealth. It is a theological rejection of the idea that Black poverty is natural, ordained, or permanent. It is an assertion of divine blessing against a history that has systematically communicated the opposite. The theology is problematic, its exegesis strained, its consequences sometimes exploitative. But the impulse behind it, the insistence that God's people deserve abundance and not merely survival, taps into something real and deeply felt.

The critique, and it is a necessary one, is that prosperity theology often individualizes what are structural problems, replacing prophetic analysis of systemic injustice with personal claims on divine favor. It can redirect energy from collective action to individual consumption. And it has made some preachers fabulously wealthy at the expense of congregations that can ill afford it. The tension between prophetic justice and prosperity theology within the Black church is real and ongoing.

Cultural Production: From Gospel to Hip-Hop

The cultural production of the Black church has shaped American culture far beyond the walls of the sanctuary. Gospel music, pioneered by Thomas A. Dorsey in the 1930s and electrified by Mahalia Jackson, the Edwin Hawkins Singers, Andrae Crouch, and Kirk Franklin, became one of the most influential musical traditions in the world. The vocal techniques of gospel, the call-and-response patterns, the emotional intensity, and the improvisational freedom flowed directly into rhythm and blues, soul, and rock and roll. Sam Cooke, Aretha Franklin, Marvin Gaye, Al Green, and Whitney Houston all came out of the church. American popular music is, to a degree rarely acknowledged, secularized Black church music.

Hip-hop's relationship to the Black church is more complicated but no less real. The prophetic tradition of speaking truth to power, of narrating the experience of the marginalized, of bearing witness to suffering and injustice, runs through hip-hop's DNA. Artists from Tupac Shakur to Kendrick Lamar have wrestled publicly with faith, sin, redemption, and divine judgment in ways that mirror the Black preaching tradition. Lamar's DAMN. is, in many ways, a sermon on the problem of theodicy. The church may not always recognize its children, but its influence is unmistakable.

What the White Church Has Never Learned

The white church in America has consistently failed to learn from the Black church, and the failure is not incidental. It is structural. To learn from the Black church would require acknowledging that the most vibrant, most prophetic, most theologically creative tradition in American Christianity emerged not from the centers of institutional power but from the margins, not from the seminaries of the privileged but from the suffering of the enslaved.

The white church has never learned that theology done from a position of comfort is always incomplete. It has never learned that worship disconnected from justice is idolatry. It has never learned that the Bible, read by the oppressed, says things that the powerful cannot hear. It has never learned that the cross is not an abstract doctrine but a political reality, that Jesus was executed by the state, and that any Christianity that consistently aligns with state power has lost the plot.

The Black church tradition insists on what the white church perpetually forgets: that Christianity is a faith born in oppression, proclaimed by the marginalized, and most authentically expressed when it speaks from below rather than from above. This is not a racial claim. It is a theological one. And it stands at the center of the New Testament, waiting to be heard by those with ears to hear.

The Ongoing Prophetic Witness

The Black church in the twenty-first century faces its own crises: generational decline in some denominations, the pull of secularism among younger Black Americans, the tension between traditional social conservatism and progressive politics, and the persistent challenge of ministering to communities devastated by mass incarceration, economic inequality, and police violence. The Movement for Black Lives, while not a church movement in the way the civil rights movement was, drew heavily on the prophetic tradition of the Black church even as it challenged the church's conservatism on issues of gender and sexuality.

But the Black church remains. It remains because it has always been more than a religious institution. It is the institutional expression of a people's determination to survive, to create beauty in the midst of brutality, to find God in the midst of godforsakenness. It is the tradition that took the slaveholder's religion and turned it into a weapon of liberation. It is the tradition that produced the spirituals, the civil rights movement, and a theology of hope that has sustained a people through four centuries of oppression.

Any Christianity that does not reckon with the Black church is an incomplete Christianity. Any theology that does not listen to voices from the underside of history is a parochial theology masquerading as universal truth. The Black church is not a subcategory of American Christianity. It is, in many ways, its most faithful expression.

chapters.title: The Consistent Pro-Life Ethic: Womb to Tomb
chapters.summary: If life is sacred because it bears the image of God, then it is sacred at every point that image is borne, and our convenient exceptions are the tell.
chapters.body:
I have stood at both ends of a human life in one week. A hospital room where a couple held the hand of a man dying of cancer, and a different room where a young mother showed me the grainy image of the child she was carrying. Both rooms made the same demand on me, and I felt it as one demand, not two. This is a person. Do not look away. The trouble is that the church, and I have been part of this, has learned to feel that demand intensely in one room and faintly in another, depending on which end of life is in front of us and which political tribe owns the question. That selective feeling is the subject here, and the diagnosis is not comfortable.

The real question is not whether human life has value. Nearly everyone says it does. The real question is whether we mean it consistently, or whether 'pro-life' has shrunk into a single-issue slogan that lets us defend the unborn fiercely while we grow cold toward the prisoner, the refugee, the poor, the condemned, and the elderly who cost us time. A principle that applies only where it is convenient is not a principle. It is a preference wearing a principle's clothes.

The strongest objection comes from thoughtful people on more than one side, and it deserves a real hearing. From one direction it runs this way. The unborn child is uniquely innocent and uniquely defenseless, and to compare abortion to debates over capital punishment or immigration or welfare policy is to dilute the gravest injustice by burying it in a list, to trade the clear killing of the innocent for a fog of contested policy questions where reasonable people differ. That is a serious point and it guards something true. Not every life issue carries the same moral weight, and the deliberate ending of an innocent life is not equivalent to a disputed question of social policy. A consistent ethic that flattens every difference would be a moral failure of its own.

But the objection, taken at its strongest, actually drives toward the consistent ethic rather than away from it, and here is why. The argument for the unborn rests on a single foundation, that this small voiceless life bears the image of God and therefore may not be destroyed for our convenience. Take that foundation seriously and it does not stay put. Carry the text that grounds it. 'So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him' (Genesis 1:27 ESV). The imago dei is the whole case for the unborn, and it is not a property that switches on at viability and off at conviction. It does not weaken with age or crime or citizenship or cost. If the image is what makes the child in the womb untouchable, then the image makes the man on death row untouchable, and the refugee at the border, and the prisoner, and the grandmother with dementia who no longer recognizes her children. The very principle that arms the defense of the unborn arms the defense of all of them. You cannot wield it selectively without cutting its edge off.

This is the argument the church has resisted, because consistency is expensive and tribal loyalty is cheap. The prophets had no such inconsistency. Their defense of life ran the full span of the vulnerable, the orphan and the widow and the poor and the foreigner, every category of the bowed-down ones, the anawim. Amos thundered against those who sold the needy for sandals. Isaiah condemned a nation whose hands were full of blood while it kept its festivals. Heschel, reading them, saw that their moral vision had no convenient exceptions. 'To us a single act of injustice is slight,' he wrote, 'to the prophets, a disaster' (Heschel 1962). A single act. Not a category we have prioritized. The prophets did not rank the vulnerable by political usefulness. Neither, it turns out, does the God they spoke for.

Trace the history and the early church holds up a mirror we would rather not look in. The Christians of the first centuries were known for refusing to take life at any point the surrounding culture took it casually. The Didache, a Christian text from around the late first century, commanded plainly, 'you shall not murder a child by abortion nor kill that which is born.' But the same Christians also defied Roman custom by rescuing infants left exposed to die, took in plague victims when pagans fled, and, in many witnesses, refused the spectacles of the arena where life was destroyed for entertainment. Their reverence did not begin and end at birth. It ran the whole span, womb to tomb, because their reverence was for the image and not for a faction's agenda. Somewhere across the centuries that consistency fractured, and in our own time it shattered along political lines, until one tribe defended the womb and abandoned the border and another defended the refugee and abandoned the womb, and both called the other a hypocrite, and both were right. I have lived inside that fracture. I have let my tribe tell me which deaths to grieve.

Here is the reversal the gospel forces on anyone honest enough to receive it. We like to imagine ourselves the defenders of life, the ones standing for the vulnerable against a careless world. Scripture asks a harder question. Whose blood is on our hands by the things we have left undone. 'Anyone who hates his brother is a murderer' (1 John 3:15 ESV). The line between the killer and the righteous defender is not as clean as our politics pretends. The God who knit the unborn child together also knit the prisoner we have stopped praying for and the enemy we have stopped seeing as human. The consistent ethic is not a burden laid on the pro-life cause from outside. It is the pro-life cause taken to its honest end, and it convicts me at the points where I had grown comfortable.

The cross does the work no slogan can. There the sacredness of life and the cost of its destruction met in one body. Christ, who bore the image of God without flaw, was put to death by a coalition of the religious and the political, condemned by a legal process and executed by the state, the most innocent life ever lived destroyed for the convenience of those it threatened. The cross shows us with unbearable clarity what it is to take an image-bearing life, and it shows it to us as our own act, for it was our sin that nailed him there. We did this. And then the cross does the thing only grace can do. The God we murdered did not return for vengeance. He returned with forgiveness, and in that forgiveness exposed the cheapness of every ethic that defends some lives to feel righteous while discarding others to feel safe. At the foot of that cross no one gets to rank the vulnerable. We are all the killers, and we are all the ones for whom he died.

So the man in the hospital bed and the child on the grainy screen make one demand, and it is the same demand the convicted man makes from his cell and the mother makes at the border. This is a person. Do not look away. The image of God does not flicker on and off according to our convenience or our voting bloc. It is borne whole, at every point a human life is borne, from the first cell to the last breath.

Womb to tomb. The whole span. No exceptions we get to keep.

### Works Cited

Heschel, Abraham J. The Prophets. New York: Harper and Row, 1962.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

chapters.title: The Eye of the Needle: Jesus and the Rich
chapters.summary: The comforting legend of a gate called the Needle's Eye was invented to soften a sentence Jesus meant to be impossible, and the impossibility is the gospel.
chapters.body:
Somewhere along the way a story got told that there was a low gate in the wall of Jerusalem called the Needle's Eye, and that a camel could squeeze through it if you unloaded its cargo and made it kneel. The point of the story was relief. See, the rich man can get in after all. He just has to stoop a little and drop some baggage. It is a tidy lesson, and it is a fabrication. There is no evidence of such a gate before the Middle Ages, when commentators invented it to relieve a pressure they could not bear. Jesus said a camel, the largest animal in Palestine, and a needle, the smallest hole anyone handled daily. He meant the largest thing and the smallest hole. He meant it cannot be done.

The real question is why we needed the gate. Why does the plain sense of this sentence frighten the church so badly that it would forge an architectural feature to escape it. The answer is that we are the rich man, and we know it, and we would rather believe in a fictional gate than face a real impossibility.

The spine here is the whole encounter, and it begins with a man running. A rich young ruler runs up to Jesus, kneels, and asks the most important question a person can ask. Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life. Jesus walks him through the commandments. The man says he has kept them all from his youth, and there is no reason to think he is lying. Then comes the hinge. Jesus, looking at him, loved him, and said, You lack one thing. Go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. And come, follow me (Mark 10:21 ESV). And the man's face falls, because he had great possessions, and he walks away sorrowful. Then Jesus turns to the disciples and says it. How difficult it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God. It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God (Mark 10:23-25 ESV).

Let me give the strong version of the reading that wants to soften this, because it is not only cowardice that produces it. The careful reader points out that Jesus does not give every rich person this command. Zacchaeus keeps half his goods and is declared saved that very day. Joseph of Arimathea is a rich man and a disciple. The text says Jesus loved this particular man and prescribed for this particular wound, that the issue was this man's heart, his specific idol, not wealth as such. On this reading the camel saying is not about money at all. It is about whatever you will not surrender, and for this man it happened to be money. The application is universal precisely because it is not really about the rich. It is about the thing you grip.

This reading is partly right, and I will not pretend otherwise. Jesus does diagnose individuals. He did love this man, and the command was tailored. Wealth is not the only idol, and the saying does press on anyone who clutches anything. All true. But notice what the gentle reading needs to ignore in order to stay gentle. Jesus does not say it is hard for a man with an idol to be saved. He says it is hard for those who have wealth. He names the category, not the heart-condition in the abstract. And when the disciples, stunned, ask then who can be saved, Jesus does not reassure them that it is really about idols in general. He widens the impossibility. With man it is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God (Mark 10:27 ESV). The softening reading turns the saying into a manageable warning about attachment. Jesus refuses to let it be managed. He drives it past difficulty into impossibility, and then He leaves it there.

Why would He do that. Because there is something about wealth in particular, not idolatry in general, that He wants named. Wealth is the idol that does not feel like one. The man who worships success feels his hunger. The man who worships a person feels his obsession. But wealth presents itself as security, as prudence, as responsibility, as love for one's family. It hides inside virtues. John Chrysostom saw this in the fourth century and would not let his comfortable congregation hide there. He told them that wealth held while a brother starved was not neutral, that the rich man who keeps what the poor man needs is not innocent but is, in the sight of God, withholding what is not finally his (Chrysostom, On Wealth and Poverty). The camel cannot fit through the needle because the camel cannot imagine it needs to. Its size is invisible to itself.

The history of how we domesticated this saying is the history of a church getting rich. In the first three centuries, before Constantine, the words still terrified. The desert fathers fled to nothing partly to escape exactly the encumbrance Jesus named. But as the church inherited the wealth of the empire, the pressure to reinterpret grew, and by the medieval period the Needle's Eye gate appears in the commentaries like a pressure valve, releasing a steam the institution could no longer contain. Tim Keller observed that the modern reflex is the same impulse in a new costume, that prosperous Western Christians have become expert at applying every hard saying about money to someone richer than themselves, so that the rich man in the story is always the next bracket up and never the man in the pew (Keller 2009). The gate moved from the wall of Jerusalem into our hermeneutics. We still build it. We just build it out of exegesis now.

Now the reversal, and it is the most important turn in this whole matter. The disciples respond to the saying with the right response, which is despair. They are exceedingly astonished and they ask, then who can be saved. And their despair is correct. That is the thing the softeners miss. The saying is supposed to crush you. It is supposed to take the man who has kept the commandments from his youth, the best man in the room, and show him he cannot purchase his way in with obedience any more than with money. The objection that the saying is too harsh, that no rich person could be saved on these terms, is not a problem to be solved. It is the door. Because the moment you stop trying to fit the camel through the needle by your own management, by unloading the right amount of baggage and kneeling the right amount, the moment you confess the thing simply cannot be done, you are finally standing where the gospel can reach you. With man it is impossible. The impossibility is not the bad news that precedes the gospel. The impossibility is the gospel's first word of truth.

This is the cross, and it stands here as law before grace, exactly. The law is the needle. It measures you and finds you too large, too laden, too sure of your own keeping of the commandments, and it does not lie. I am the camel. I have possessions I have justified, securities I have called prudence, a comfort I would be slow to sell even to follow the One I claim to follow. The law names me before it names the man who walked away sorrowful. And then grace. The One who said it is impossible is the One who went up to Jerusalem to make the impossible happen, who became poor that we by His poverty might become rich, who was Himself the only one who could pass through the needle and chose instead to be threaded onto a Roman cross so that camels like me could follow Him through. The man walked away because he thought the price was his wealth. The price was higher than that. The price was everything, and it was paid by someone else.

So what do we do with the rich young ruler, we who are, by every global measure, richer than he ever dreamed. We stop building the gate. We let the sentence stand at its full impossible height. We let it take the breath out of us the way it took the breath out of the disciples. And then, having despaired of fitting through on our own terms, we look up at the only One for whom all things are possible, and we hear the same command the rich man heard, the command he could not obey and we cannot either, except that now it comes from a Savior who has already gone ahead of us through the needle He alone could pass.

The man went away sorrowful. The text does not tell us he never came back. I have hoped, in more than one quiet moment, that he did. That somewhere after the cross he heard that the thing he could not do had been done for him, and that he came back, lighter now, not because he had finally unloaded enough, but because he had finally stopped trying to fit and let himself be carried.

### Works Cited

John Chrysostom. On Wealth and Poverty. Translated by Catharine P. Roth. Crestwood: St. Vladimir's Seminary Press, 1984.

Keller, Timothy. Counterfeit Gods: The Empty Promises of Money, Sex, and Power, and the Only Hope That Matters. New York: Dutton, 2009.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

chapters.title: The Image of God and the Lie of Race
chapters.summary: Race is a recent invention dressed up as an ancient fact, and the church helped sew the costume.
chapters.body:
Ask a child where race comes from and she will tell you it has always been here, that people simply are these colors and these kinds, the way the sky is blue. Ask a historian and you get a different answer. Race as we mean it, the sorting of humanity into a ladder of worth by the color of skin, is younger than the printing press. It was made. And the making has a date, a motive, and a set of hands, and some of those hands held a Bible.

The text I want to carry is the oldest claim Scripture makes about a human being. God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him, male and female he created them (Genesis 1:27 ESV). The imago dei. Before nation, before tribe, before anything we call race, there is this. Every human being bears the image of God, and that image is not distributed by degree. It is not more present in one people and less in another. It is the floor under all of us, the thing that makes a person a person, and Scripture lays it down in the first chapter before sin has even entered the story.

Here is the strong objection, and I want it stated at full strength. Many thoughtful people say the church should stop talking about race entirely, that the very category is the problem, that to keep naming Black and white is to keep alive a fiction we should let die. Color blindness, they argue, is the Christian position. We are all one in Christ, there is neither Jew nor Greek, so why keep sorting the body by a distinction the gospel abolished. There is something genuinely right in this, and I will not pretend otherwise. The category of race is a lie. It has no basis in biology. The differences we have built a ladder upon are surface deep, and the gospel really does make one new humanity out of the many.

But here is where the color-blind answer fails, and it fails for a reason worth understanding. You cannot heal a wound by refusing to name the weapon. Race is a lie, yes. But it is a lie that built a world, that wrote laws, that drew maps, that decided who got a loan and who got a noose, and you do not undo a four-hundred-year-old structure by closing your eyes to it. Telling a man whose grandfather was redlined out of a neighborhood that you do not see color does not return the house. It only blinds you to why he does not have one. The lie of race must be named precisely because it is a lie that did real damage, and the damage did not vanish when we stopped saying the quiet part out loud.

Trace the invention. Before the European slave trade, people knew themselves by tribe, by city, by faith, by tongue. There were enslaved people of every shade, and slavery, evil as it was, was not yet organized around color. Then came the seventeenth century and a problem the planters needed to solve. African labor was being held for life while European labor was held for years, and that difference needed a justification that could survive a Christian conscience. So the category was built. Willie James Jennings shows how European Christians, in the age of conquest, began to read the peoples of the earth through a new lens, with whiteness placed at the top as the measure of the human and Blackness at the bottom, and how theology lent its weight to the sorting (Jennings 2010). Race was not discovered. It was theologically manufactured to make a sin look like an order of creation.

The church did not merely permit this. It supplied the verses. The so-called curse of Ham, drawn from a misreading of Genesis 9, was preached for centuries as the divine charter for African slavery, the claim that a whole people had been cursed to servitude by the word of God. It was a lie laid on top of the lie of race, Scripture twisted to baptize an economy. Esau McCaulley, reading the Bible from within the Black church tradition, shows how the same texts the slaveholder weaponized were read by the enslaved as a charter of dignity and deliverance, how Reading While Black means refusing both the oppressor's distortion and the despair it was meant to produce (McCaulley 2020). The book that was used to forge the chain was the same book that named the prisoner an image-bearer. Only one of those readings was true.

Here is the reversal, and it is the heart of the matter. We tend to think the problem of race is a problem of difference, that if we could only see past our differences we would be at peace. But Genesis says the opposite. The problem is not that we are different. God made the difference and called the whole creation very good. The problem is that we took a difference God made and built a hierarchy God never authorized. The sin is not color. The sin is the ladder. And the cure for a ladder is not to pretend everyone is on the same rung by ignoring the ranks. The cure is to tear the ladder down and confess we built it.

The imago dei does real work here, and it does it as law before it does it as grace. As law, it indicts. If every human bears the image of God, then every act of the slave trade, every lynching, every redlined map, every sermon that ranked the races was an assault on the image of God, a defacing of his likeness in the person of his neighbor. There is no neutral ground. To diminish a human being by color is to spit on the face of God reflected in that human being, and the church that taught the diminishing taught blasphemy with a Bible open. I am in that church's lineage. So is every white believer in America. The indictment includes us.

And as grace, the imago dei restores. The image cannot be erased by any lie. Four hundred years of teaching that Black bodies were worth less did not make them worth less, because worth was never ours to assign. It was set by God in the first chapter and sealed by God in the incarnation, when the Word took on flesh and dignified the human body forever. Augustine wrote that the image of God in us, defaced by sin, is being renewed in those who turn to Christ, restored to the likeness it was made for (Augustine, The Trinity 14). The lie of race tried to deface the image. The gospel renews it. And a church renewed in the image of God cannot keep the ladder. The renewal and the ladder cannot stand in the same body.

So we do not get color blindness, and we do not get the ladder either. We get something harder than both. We get the call to name the lie for what it is, to confess the hands that made it, and to look at every human face, including the faces our fathers ranked, and see what was always there.

The image of God. Defaced for four centuries. Never once erased.

### Works Cited

Augustine. The Trinity. Translated by Edmund Hill. Brooklyn: New City Press, 1991.

Jennings, Willie James. The Christian Imagination: Theology and the Origins of Race. New Haven: Yale University Press, 2010.

McCaulley, Esau. Reading While Black: African American Biblical Interpretation as an Exercise in Hope. Downers Grove: InterVarsity Press, 2020.

chapters.title: The Megachurch Model: What Worked, What Didn't, What's Next
chapters.summary: The megachurch movement reached millions and revealed something important about American Christianity's hunger for accessibility. It also revealed something about what happens when the church mistakes growth for faithfulness.
chapters.body:
In 1975, Bill Hybels rented a movie theater in Palatine, Illinois, and launched a church service designed for people who did not go to church. He had conducted door-to-door surveys in the surrounding suburbs, asking unchurched residents what they disliked about church. Their answers were consistent: it was boring, irrelevant, always asking for money, and made them feel guilty. Hybels built Willow Creek Community Church as the answer to those objections. The music was contemporary. The messages were practical. The atmosphere was welcoming, nonthreatening, and intentionally modeled on the spaces where suburban Americans already felt comfortable — corporate auditoriums, shopping malls, entertainment venues.

It worked. Willow Creek grew to over twenty-five thousand weekly attendees. It became the prototype for a movement. Rick Warren applied similar principles at Saddleback Church in Lake Forest, California, which grew to comparable size and produced The Purpose Driven Life, one of the best-selling nonfiction books in American history. By the early 2000s, the megachurch model — defined as a church with weekly attendance of two thousand or more — had spread across the country. The Hartford Institute for Religion Research counted over seventeen hundred megachurches in the United States by 2020, a number that had more than doubled since 2000.

The megachurch movement was the most significant development in American Protestant Christianity in the second half of the twentieth century. It reshaped the terrain of American religion, the expectations of churchgoers, the economics of ministry, and the culture of pastoral leadership. It did some things remarkably well. It did other things catastrophically badly. And the reckoning that followed has forced a conversation about what the church is actually for — a conversation that is still far from resolved.

What Worked

The megachurch movement's most significant achievement was accessibility. For millions of Americans who had been alienated by traditional church culture — its unfamiliar rituals, its insider language, its assumption that newcomers already knew the rules — the megachurch offered a genuine on-ramp.
