You could walk in without knowing anything about Christianity and not feel stupid, excluded, or judged. The music was in a key you recognized. The sermon addressed problems you actually had. The building looked like a place where normal people gathered, not a medieval artifact that required a guide.

This accessibility was not superficial. It represented a serious theological commitment: the belief that the gospel is for everyone, and that the church bears responsibility for removing unnecessary barriers to encounter. The seeker-sensitive movement, at its best, was an exercise in contextual theology — translating the message of Christianity into the vernacular of contemporary American culture without compromising its substance. Paul did this in Athens. The Jesuits did it in China. Hybels and Warren did it in the suburbs.

The megachurch also excelled at organizational excellence. Whatever criticisms can be leveled at the movement, it is difficult to argue that the average megachurch was not better organized, better managed, and more intentional about its operations than the average small church. Volunteer coordination, children's ministry, facility management, communication — the megachurch brought a level of institutional competence to these functions that smaller churches often lacked. For families with young children, in particular, the difference was palpable. A well-run children's ministry, a clean and safe facility, a service that started on time — these things matter, and the megachurch delivered them consistently.

The movement also demonstrated the power of strategic thinking about mission. The megachurch leaders were, for all their flaws, deeply serious about reaching people outside the church. They thought carefully about demographics, communication, cultural barriers, and the psychology of spiritual seeking. They approached evangelism not as a duty performed through guilt but as a strategic enterprise that deserved the same level of planning and investment as any other serious undertaking.

What Didn't Work

The megachurch model contained structural flaws that became visible only over time — flaws that were not incidental to the model but embedded in its foundational assumptions.

The first flaw was the celebrity pastor. The megachurch, by its nature, concentrates enormous attention, authority, and resources in a single leader. The senior pastor becomes the brand. The church's identity, its growth, its financial viability, and its public reputation are all tethered to one person. This structure creates conditions that are almost perfectly designed to produce the pathologies of celebrity: isolation, entitlement, unaccountability, the gradual erosion of the boundary between the leader's identity and the institution's mission.

The Willow Creek Association, which Hybels founded to export the megachurch model to churches worldwide, marketed not just a methodology but a personality. When Hybels was accused of sexual harassment and misconduct — allegations that were eventually substantiated by an independent investigation — the entire enterprise was compromised. The model had no mechanism for holding its central figure accountable because the central figure was the model.

The second flaw was consumer Christianity. The seeker-sensitive approach, which began as a missiological strategy, gradually became a market strategy. The church adopted the logic of the marketplace: the congregation as customer base, the sermon as product, the worship service as experience to be consumed. Satisfaction surveys replaced confession. Preference became the organizing principle of ministry. Churches competed for market share — not consciously, perhaps, but functionally — by offering better programming, more convenient services, superior production values.

The result was a form of Christianity shaped more by consumer preference than by the costly demands of discipleship. The megachurch excelled at attracting people. It struggled to form them. Willow Creek's own internal research, published in the 2007 study Reveal, acknowledged this problem with surprising candor: the church had been more effective at creating consumers of religious programming than disciples of Jesus Christ. The most spiritually mature members, the study found, were the least satisfied — because the church had been designed for seekers, not for saints.

The third flaw was shallow discipleship. The megachurch service, optimized for accessibility, often achieved accessibility at the expense of depth. Sermons were practical, relevant, and application-oriented — but they frequently lacked theological substance. Complex doctrines were simplified to the point of distortion. The Bible was mined for principles rather than encountered as a text. The liturgical traditions of the church — the creeds, the sacraments, the rhythms of the church year — were jettisoned as barriers to accessibility, and with them went centuries of accumulated wisdom about how to form the human soul.

The megachurch asked the right question: How do we reach people who are not here? But it failed to ask the harder question: What do we do with them once they arrive?

The Reckoning

The scandals that engulfed megachurch leaders in the 2010s and 2020s were not isolated incidents. They were structural consequences of the model itself. Bill Hybels at Willow Creek. Mark Driscoll at Mars Hill. Carl Lentz at Hillsong New York. James MacDonald at Harvest Bible Chapel. Each case followed the same arc: a charismatic leader builds a massive institution around his personality, concentrates authority in himself, marginalizes or eliminates internal accountability, and eventually falls — taking the institution, or large parts of it, down with him.

Driscoll's case is particularly instructive. Mars Hill Church in Seattle grew from a handful of people to over fourteen thousand weekly attendees in fifteen years. Driscoll's aggressive, confrontational style — described by Christianity Today as "the cussing pastor" — attracted young men in numbers that few other churches could match. But the same authoritarianism that drove the church's growth eventually destroyed it. Former elders described a culture of fear, bullying, and spiritual abuse. When the church's board attempted to hold Driscoll accountable, he resigned and the church collapsed, closing all of its campuses within months.

Lentz at Hillsong was fired for "moral failures" — a euphemism that later expanded into a broader picture of a church culture built on celebrity, image management, and the systematic prioritization of the brand over the well-being of staff and congregants. MacDonald at Harvest was removed after recordings surfaced of him making vulgar, racially insensitive, and threatening remarks — but only after years of financial misconduct, bullying of staff, and suppression of dissent that the church's governance structures had failed to address.

The pattern is not coincidental. It is architectural. Build a church around a personality. Give that personality unchecked authority. Remove the structural safeguards — elder boards with real power, financial transparency, congregational governance — that might constrain that authority. And wait. The fall is not guaranteed, but the conditions for it are. The megachurch model, as commonly practiced, is a machine for producing exactly the kind of leadership failures it has produced.

What Comes Next

The post-megachurch reality is still emerging, but its contours are becoming visible. The movement is not dying — megachurches continue to exist and, in some cases, to thrive. But the assumptions that drove the movement are being questioned in ways they have not been before, and the alternatives being explored suggest a significant shift in what American Protestantism considers a healthy church.

Smaller is being reconsidered. The assumption that bigger is better — that numerical growth is the primary indicator of ministerial health — is being challenged by a growing number of pastors, theologians, and church planters who argue that the most significant work of the church happens at a scale that megachurches cannot reach. Relationships of genuine depth. Mutual accountability. The slow, patient work of formation that requires a pastor who knows your name, your story, your struggles — not a communicator on a stage who delivers content to an audience.

Deeper is being prioritized. The reaction against seeker-sensitive shallowness has produced a renewed interest in theological depth, liturgical richness, and the formative practices of the historic church. Young evangelicals are discovering the church fathers, the Book of Common Prayer, the contemplative tradition, the rhythms of the church year. They are hungry not for relevance but for rootedness — not for a Christianity that accommodates the culture but for one that offers a genuine alternative to it.

More accountable structures are being designed. The celebrity pastor model is being replaced, in some quarters, by team leadership, plural eldership, and governance structures that distribute authority rather than concentrating it. Churches are implementing financial transparency, independent audits, and formal accountability mechanisms that do not depend on the goodwill of the leader being held accountable.

None of this guarantees a better outcome. Small churches can be abusive. Liturgical churches can be shallow. Accountability structures can be performative. The problem is not merely structural but spiritual — rooted in the human capacity for self-deception and the institutional tendency toward self-preservation. But the megachurch era has taught the American church something it needed to learn: that growth is not the same as health, that efficiency is not the same as faithfulness, and that the size of the crowd tells you nothing about the depth of the formation happening within it.

The church Jesus described — a community of mutual service, sacrificial love, genuine accountability, and radical commitment to the way of the cross — has never been efficiently scalable. That may be the point.

chapters.title: The Most Segregated Hour: Why Sunday Morning Is Still Divided
chapters.summary: The hour we call holy is the hour we keep apart, and the building of that wall has a history older than our discomfort with naming it.
chapters.body:
Martin Luther King Jr. said it, and we have been quoting him ever since as if quoting him were the same as repenting. Eleven o'clock on Sunday morning, he said, is the most segregated hour in America. We nod. We put the line on a slide behind the worship leader. Then we drive home to the same neighborhood we drove from, to the same church we have always attended, and nothing about Monday morning is different from Saturday night.

The sociologists confirm what King saw. Michael Emerson and Christian Smith, in their 2000 study Divided by Faith, found that a congregation counts as multiracial only when no single group exceeds eighty percent of the membership, and by that low bar fewer than one in ten American churches qualified. The number has crept upward since. It has not moved far. The most segregated hour is still the most segregated hour, and we have grown comfortable enough with the diagnosis that we no longer feel the wound.

There is a serious objection to make here, and I want to make it well before I answer it. Some say the church talks about race too much already, that the constant return to this subject has politicized the pulpit, baptized a partisan agenda, and turned the gospel into a program of social management. They say people of every background already worship freely, that the doors are open, that nobody is turned away, that segregation by preference is not segregation by law and the two should never be confused. They are right about something real. The gospel is not a political platform. A church that preaches a party has lost the cross. And the people who fill our pews on Sunday are not standing at a barred door. No usher checks their skin.

But the open door is not the whole truth, and the people who say it know it is not. Preference did not fall from the sky. Preference was built. The text I want to carry through this is short and it does not flatter us. In Christ, Paul writes, God has broken down the dividing wall of hostility, has made the two groups one, has created in himself one new humanity in place of the two, thus making peace (Ephesians 2:14-15 ESV). Paul is not describing a feeling. He is describing a demolition. There was a wall in the temple, a literal partition past which a Gentile could not go on pain of death, and Paul says the cross tore it down. The question for us is not whether the wall is gone in heaven. The question is who keeps rebuilding it on earth, and the answer includes me.

Trace it back. The dividing wall in American Christianity was not an accident of geography. In 1845 the Baptists split into North and South over whether a slaveholder could be a missionary, and the Southern Baptist Convention was born to defend a man's right to own a man and call himself sent by God. The Methodists had split the year before. The Presbyterians would fracture too. The largest churches in the land organized themselves around the keeping of human beings as property, and they did it with open Bibles. Jemar Tisby calls this the color of compromise, the long record of a church that did not merely fail to resist racism but actively constructed it (Tisby 2019). The wall in our sanctuaries is the same wall. We did not inherit a neutral silence. We inherited a structure.

After slavery came the next layer. Black Christians who had sat in the balconies of white churches walked out and built their own, not from preference but from refusal, the refusal of white congregations to seat them as equals at the same table. The Black church in America is in large part a monument to white Christian rejection. Then came the federal redlining maps of the 1930s, the restrictive housing covenants, the highways routed through Black neighborhoods, the suburbs sold to whites only. By the time King named it, the segregated hour was the natural fruit of a hundred years of deliberate sorting. We did not choose it on a given Sunday. Our grandparents chose it across a century, and we have not chosen against it.

Howard Thurman saw the cost from inside. In Jesus and the Disinherited, written in 1949, he asks what the religion of Jesus has to say to those with their backs against the wall, and he records the searing question his own grandmother, born enslaved, put to the faith she was handed. Why would she keep a book that had been used to keep her down. Thurman's answer is that the religion of the slaveholder and the religion of Jesus are not the same religion, that one blesses the wall and the other breaks it (Thurman 1949). The tragedy is that they wore the same name and met in the same hour, and to the watching world they were indistinguishable.

Here is the reversal. We treat the segregated hour as a problem of comfort, as if the solution were to make worship a little more varied so everyone feels welcome. But Ephesians does not aim at comfort. The wall Paul names is a wall of hostility, and the cross does not redecorate it. The cross kills the hostility (Ephesians 2:16 ESV). That is violent language and it is meant to be. The thing standing between us is not difference. Difference is the gift of God, every tongue and tribe a facet of his glory. The thing standing between us is enmity, and enmity does not yield to a friendlier greeting at the door. It yields to death, the death of the old humanity that needed the wall to feel safe.

So the law comes before the grace, and the law is this. We built the wall. The white church in America, my church, the tradition I serve in, laid every course of brick with Scripture in hand, and the fact that the mortar has dried and we no longer remember mixing it does not make us innocent. To say the door is open while standing in a building our fathers designed to keep certain people in the balcony is to mistake the absence of a new crime for the presence of repentance. We have not torn down the wall. We have stopped noticing it.

And here is the grace, which is harder than the comfort we wanted. The cross has already done the demolition. Paul does not command us to build one new humanity. He announces that God has made it, past tense, finished, in the body of Christ. Our task is not construction. It is to stop maintaining the ruin. To walk into the hour we have kept apart and refuse, with our feet and our budgets and our pulpits and our friendships, to keep it apart any longer. That is not a program. It is obedience to something already true.

King's line was never meant to be a lament we recite. It was meant to be a verdict we answered. We have recited it for sixty years. The hour is still divided. The wall is down in heaven and standing in our sanctuaries, and the hands holding it up are our own.

### Works Cited

Emerson, Michael O., and Christian Smith. Divided by Faith: Evangelical Religion and the Problem of Race in America. New York: Oxford University Press, 2000.

Thurman, Howard. Jesus and the Disinherited. Boston: Beacon Press, 1949.

Tisby, Jemar. The Color of Compromise: The Truth about the American Church's Complicity in Racism. Grand Rapids: Zondervan, 2019.

chapters.title: The Sexual Abuse Crisis: A Reckoning the Church Cannot Avoid
chapters.summary: The abuse crisis is not a Catholic problem or a Protestant problem. It is a power problem. And until the church names the structural conditions that produce predators and protect them, it will keep producing both.
chapters.body:
In January 2002, the Boston Globe's Spotlight team published the first of a series of investigative reports documenting the systematic sexual abuse of children by Catholic priests in the Archdiocese of Boston. The reporting revealed that Cardinal Bernard Law and his predecessors had known about the abuse for decades. They had not merely failed to stop it. They had actively enabled it — transferring accused priests to new parishes, suppressing complaints, pressuring victims into silence, deploying church lawyers to intimidate families who came forward. The institution had chosen its reputation over its children.

The Boston reporting was not the beginning. Allegations had surfaced for years — in Louisiana in the 1980s, in documents uncovered by attorney Jeff Anderson, in the courageous testimonies of survivors who were dismissed as liars or opportunists. But the Globe's investigation achieved what individual complaints had not: it established a pattern. Not isolated cases. Not a few bad actors. A system. A system designed, at every level, to protect the institution at the expense of the vulnerable.

What followed was a global reckoning. Grand jury reports in Pennsylvania documented over a thousand child victims and three hundred predator priests across six dioceses, spanning seven decades. Investigations in Ireland, Australia, Germany, Chile, and dozens of other countries revealed the same architecture of abuse and concealment. The case of Theodore McCarrick — a cardinal, one of the most powerful figures in American Catholicism — demonstrated that the rot reached the highest levels of church leadership. McCarrick had abused seminarians and minors for decades while ascending to positions of extraordinary influence. People knew. The institution knew. It advanced him anyway.

The Protestant Reckoning

For years, many Protestants watched the Catholic crisis with a mixture of horror and self-congratulation. The problem, they told themselves, was celibacy. The problem was hierarchy. The problem was a closed institutional culture unique to Rome. They were wrong on every count.

In 2022, the Southern Baptist Convention released the findings of an independent investigation conducted by Guidepost Solutions. The report documented a pattern of abuse, cover-up, and institutional self-protection that mirrored the Catholic crisis in its essential features. The SBC's Executive Committee had maintained a secret list of accused abusers while publicly resisting calls to create a database or implement safeguards. Leaders who advocated for survivors were marginalized. Christa Brown, who had spent years pressing the SBC to act, was dismissed and demeaned by the very leaders charged with protecting the vulnerable. The Guidepost report revealed internal communications in which SBC leaders discussed strategies not for addressing abuse but for avoiding legal liability.

The SBC was not alone. Willow Creek Community Church — once the flagship of the American megachurch movement — faced its own crisis when founder Bill Hybels was accused of sexual harassment and misconduct spanning decades. The church's initial response was to defend Hybels, attack his accusers, and circle the institutional wagons. An independent investigation eventually substantiated the allegations, but only after years of institutional resistance and incalculable damage to the women who came forward.

Ravi Zacharias, perhaps the most prominent Christian apologist of his generation, was posthumously revealed to have engaged in a sustained pattern of sexual abuse, including the abuse of massage therapists at spas he owned. His organization, RZIM, had received complaints during his lifetime and failed to investigate them meaningfully. After his death, an independent investigation documented the scope of his predation. The organization that bore his name eventually shut down — but only after decades of institutional complicity.

The pattern extends to independent churches, parachurch organizations, mission agencies, and Christian schools. Sovereign Grace Churches faced allegations of systematic abuse cover-up. The Institute in Basic Life Principles, founded by Bill Gothard, protected its leader despite years of sexual harassment complaints. Bob Jones University hired an independent firm to investigate its handling of sexual abuse — then fired the firm when its findings became uncomfortable. The list is long. It is still growing.

The Structure That Produces the Pattern

Individual predators exist in every institution. What distinguishes the church's abuse crisis is not the existence of abusers but the structural conditions that enable them and the institutional reflexes that protect them. These conditions are identifiable. They are predictable. And they are, in most churches, still firmly in place.

The first condition is unaccountable authority. Churches that concentrate spiritual authority in a single leader — and that teach congregants to equate questioning that leader with questioning God — create the perfect environment for abuse. When a pastor is treated as God's anointed representative, challenging his behavior becomes an act of spiritual rebellion. Victims who come forward are not merely disbelieved. They are recast as enemies of the faith.

The second condition is theological manipulation. Abusers in church settings routinely weaponize the language of faith to silence their victims. Forgiveness becomes a tool of coercion: victims are told that a failure to forgive their abuser is a sin. Submission becomes a mechanism of control: women and children are taught that obedience to authority is obedience to God. Grace becomes a shield for the perpetrator: calls for accountability are reframed as failures of Christian charity.

The third condition is institutional self-preservation. When an organization believes it is doing God's work, any threat to the organization's reputation becomes, in the distorted logic of institutional theology, a threat to God's work. Protecting the institution is reframed as protecting the mission. Silencing a victim is reframed as preventing scandal that would harm the gospel. The institution's survival becomes the highest good, and individual victims are sacrificed on its altar.

The church did not merely fail to protect the vulnerable. It constructed theological justifications for leaving them unprotected. That is not a failure of implementation. It is a failure of theology.

What Mandatory Reporting Means and Why Churches Resist It

In most U.S. states, clergy are mandatory reporters — legally required to report suspected child abuse to civil authorities. In practice, compliance is inconsistent. Many states include clergy exemptions when the information is obtained through confidential communications such as confession or pastoral counseling. Some denominations have actively lobbied to preserve these exemptions.

The resistance to mandatory reporting reveals a deeper theological problem. It rests on the assumption that the church's internal processes — pastoral care, church discipline, denominational oversight — are sufficient to address abuse. They are not. Church discipline is designed for matters of spiritual accountability among consenting adults. It is structurally incapable of addressing criminal behavior, protecting victims from ongoing harm, or ensuring that predators face legal consequences. When a church handles abuse internally, it is not exercising spiritual authority. It is obstructing justice.

Every church, regardless of denomination or polity, should adopt a clear, unambiguous policy: all suspected abuse is reported to civil authorities immediately. Not after an internal investigation. Not after consulting with denominational lawyers. Not after praying about it. Immediately. The safety of a child is not a matter for ecclesiastical deliberation.

Independent Investigations: Why They Matter

Churches cannot investigate themselves. This should be obvious, but it is a lesson the church has been extraordinarily slow to learn. When an institution investigates allegations against its own leaders, using its own personnel, following its own procedures, the outcome is predetermined. The investigation exists not to uncover truth but to manage liability.

Independent investigations — conducted by qualified professionals with no institutional loyalty, full access to documents and personnel, and a mandate to publish their findings — are the minimum standard of accountability. The Guidepost investigation of the SBC demonstrated what independent scrutiny can accomplish: it uncovered what decades of internal processes had concealed. The Pennsylvania grand jury reports accomplished what diocesan review boards had not.

The church's resistance to independent investigation is itself diagnostic. An institution confident in its integrity welcomes scrutiny. An institution that fights investigation is telling you, in the clearest possible terms, what it expects the investigation to find.

Victim-Centered Policy

The phrase "victim-centered" is not a concession to contemporary therapeutic culture. It is a theological imperative. The God revealed in Scripture is consistently, relentlessly oriented toward the vulnerable. The prophets measured the faithfulness of Israel not by the magnificence of its worship but by its treatment of the widow, the orphan, the stranger. Jesus reserved his most severe condemnation not for sinners but for religious leaders who burdened the vulnerable and failed to protect the weak. "If anyone causes one of these little ones to stumble," he said, "it would be better for them to have a large millstone hung around their neck and to be drowned in the depths of the sea." That is not a metaphor. It is a verdict.

Victim-centered policy means that when an allegation of abuse is made, the institution's first question is not "How do we protect our reputation?" but "How do we protect this person?" It means believing survivors as a starting posture, not as a conclusion reached only after exhaustive institutional self-defense. It means providing material support — counseling, legal assistance, financial help — to those who have been harmed, without requiring them to sign nondisclosure agreements or waive their right to pursue justice. It means removing accused leaders from positions of authority immediately and permanently, regardless of their institutional value.

It means, in short, treating the vulnerable the way Jesus treated the vulnerable. Which is to say: as the point of the entire enterprise.

What Genuine Repentance Looks Like

The church has become skilled at performing repentance without practicing it. Press conferences are held. Statements are issued. The language of sorrow is deployed with professional precision. And then the institution returns to its prior operations with minimal structural change. This is not repentance. It is public relations.

Genuine repentance in the context of institutional abuse requires, at minimum, the following: a full and honest accounting of what happened, conducted by independent investigators and made public without redaction. Direct, personal accountability for leaders who enabled or concealed abuse, including removal from positions of authority and, where applicable, cooperation with criminal prosecution. Material restitution to survivors — not as a legal settlement designed to minimize liability but as an act of justice. Permanent structural changes to governance, accountability, and oversight that make future abuse more difficult and future concealment impossible.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer distinguished between "cheap grace" and "costly grace." Cheap grace is grace without repentance, forgiveness without restitution, absolution without accountability. The church's response to the abuse crisis has been, overwhelmingly, an exercise in cheap grace — grace extended to the institution and its leaders, paid for by the suffering of victims who were told to forgive and move on.

Costly grace demands more. It demands that the institution bear the full weight of what it has done. It demands that leaders who failed be held accountable, not shuffled to new positions. It demands that survivors be heard, believed, and compensated — not as an act of institutional generosity but as the minimum requirement of justice. It demands that the church become, in its structures and practices, the kind of institution where abuse is not merely condemned in sermons but made structurally impossible.

We are not there. We are not close. The church has named the sin in the abstract while protecting the sinners in the particular. It has called for repentance while resisting the concrete changes repentance demands. It has wept publicly while fighting privately to preserve the structures that made the crisis possible.

The reckoning is not optional. It is not a phase the church can wait out. It is the work of a generation — or it is the end of the church's moral credibility in the culture it claims to serve. Those are the only two options. There is no third way.

chapters.title: Toxic Masculinity in the Pulpit
chapters.summary: The church that confuses aggression with authority and domination with leadership has not recovered biblical manhood. It has baptized the very thing the gospel came to crucify.
chapters.body:
In 2006, Mark Driscoll stood before a conference of pastors and declared that the problem with the American church was that it had become too feminine. The church needed men, he argued — real men, tough men, men who would fight and lead and dominate. He mocked pastors who were gentle, who wept, who preferred diplomacy to confrontation. He described Jesus as a cage fighter, an alpha male, a warrior who would return at the end of days to deliver divine violence. The message was clear: godly manhood was aggressive, confrontational, and unapologetically dominant. Anything else was weakness. Anything else was feminization. Anything else was failure.

Driscoll was not an outlier. He was the loudest voice in a movement that had been building for decades — a movement that defined masculinity in terms of power, authority, and control, and that located these qualities at the center of God's design for men. John Eldredge's Wild at Heart, published in 2001 and eventually selling over four million copies, told men that they were designed to be warriors, adventurers, and rescuers — and that the modern church, with its emphasis on gentleness, servanthood, and emotional vulnerability, had stolen their masculine identity. The Council on Biblical Manhood and Womanhood, founded in 1987, codified a vision of gender in which male leadership and female submission were presented as the eternal, unchangeable order of creation.

The result was a theology of masculinity that bore almost no resemblance to the man at the center of the Christian story. It looked, instead, remarkably like the cultural ideal of the American alpha male — competitive, dominant, emotionally controlled, sexually aggressive — dressed in theological clothing and marketed as God's original design.

The Driscoll Playbook

Mark Driscoll built Mars Hill Church in Seattle from a handful of people meeting in a living room to over fourteen thousand weekly attendees in fifteen years. His appeal was concentrated among young men — a demographic that most churches struggled to reach. He succeeded by offering them a Christianity that affirmed the version of masculinity they already held: aggressive, competitive, uncompromising, and contemptuous of softness in any form.

Driscoll's preaching was laced with the language of domination. He publicly humiliated men he considered insufficiently masculine. He described stay-at-home fathers as failures. He joked about men who displayed emotion. He wielded theological authority as a weapon, framing disagreement with his leadership as rebellion against God. Former elders and staff members have described a culture of intimidation, bullying, and spiritual coercion in which Driscoll's word was effectively law and dissent was treated as disloyalty.

The Mars Hill experiment ended in 2014, when the accumulated weight of Driscoll's behavior — plagiarism, financial impropriety, bullying, abuse of authority — finally exceeded what the institution could sustain. The church dissolved. Its campuses closed. Thousands of members were scattered, many of them deeply wounded by an experience they had been told was biblical Christianity.

But Driscoll did not disappear. He moved to Arizona and planted a new church, which grew rapidly. The market for his version of masculinity had not diminished. It had, if anything, expanded — fueled by a broader cultural anxiety about masculinity that Driscoll was positioned to exploit. The pattern repeated itself, with new allegations of authoritarian leadership, staff abuse, and institutional control emerging from the new church. The product had not changed. It did not need to. The demand was still there.

The Warrior-Poet Myth

Eldredge's Wild at Heart offered a softer version of the same essential message. Men, Eldredge argued, are hardwired for three things: a battle to fight, an adventure to live, and a beauty to rescue. These desires are not cultural constructions but divine implants — the fingerprints of God on the male soul. The modern church, Eldredge argued, had domesticated men, turning them into "really nice guys" who had lost touch with their primal masculine energy.

The appeal is understandable. Many men in the church do feel that their experience is not reflected in the prevailing culture of evangelical Christianity — a culture that often emphasizes emotional expression, relational intimacy, and gentle compliance in ways that feel foreign to their lived experience of masculinity. Eldredge gave these men permission to be something other than domesticated — to embrace risk, physicality, and strength as features, not bugs, of their masculine design.

The problem is not the affirmation of masculine energy per se. The problem is the definition of masculine energy that Eldredge assumes. The warrior-poet framework draws its vision of manhood not from the life of Christ but from romantic mythology, Hollywood action narratives, and Jungian archetypes. The "battle" is framed in terms of conquest and competition. The "adventure" is framed in terms of individual heroism. The "beauty" is framed in terms of rescue — positioning women as objects to be saved rather than agents in their own right. The entire framework is self-referential: it centers male experience, male desire, and male self-actualization. The other — whether woman, neighbor, or God — exists primarily as a mirror for the man's heroic arc.

Jesus does not appear in this framework except as an afterthought — a divine endorsement of the masculine ideal the author has already constructed. And the Jesus who does appear is selectively edited: the Jesus who overturned tables makes the cut, but the Jesus who washed feet does not. The Jesus who confronted the Pharisees makes the cut, but the Jesus who wept at Lazarus's tomb is treated as an anomaly rather than a revelation.

What Biblical Manhood Actually Looks Like

The New Testament presents a vision of manhood that is, by the standards of both first-century Mediterranean culture and twenty-first-century American culture, profoundly countercultural. It does not affirm the alpha-male ideal. It crucifies it.

Jesus wept. Publicly. At the tomb of a friend. In a culture where male tears were a sign of weakness, Jesus wept without apology, without explanation, without the macho caveat that he was only crying because he was about to do something powerful. He wept because his friend was dead and grief was the appropriate response to death. The Son of God modeled emotional vulnerability as an expression of strength, not a lapse from it.

Jesus washed feet. The act of a slave — the lowest act of service in the ancient household — performed by the one who held all authority. He knelt before his disciples, took off his outer garment, and did the work that no self-respecting man would do. And when Peter objected — when Peter displayed the masculine instinct to refuse the humiliation of being served — Jesus told him that unless he accepted it, he had no part in the kingdom. The kingdom's definition of greatness was not power exercised over others but service rendered to others. "The greatest among you shall be your servant," Jesus said. He was not speaking metaphorically.

Jesus refused violence. In the Garden of Gethsemane, when Peter drew a sword to defend him, Jesus told him to put it away. "Those who live by the sword will die by the sword." He submitted to arrest, trial, torture, and execution without resistance — not because he lacked power but because the kingdom he embodied operated on fundamentally different terms than the kingdoms of the world. The cross is not a warrior's victory. It is a servant's sacrifice. And it is the central symbol of the faith that the toxic masculinity movement claims to represent.

Paul's vision of manhood is consistent with Jesus' example. The fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control — reads like a deliberate inversion of the warrior-male ideal. Gentleness is listed as a spiritual virtue, not a feminine weakness. Self-control is valued over aggression. Patience is prized over decisive action. The man shaped by the Spirit looks nothing like the man shaped by the Driscoll playbook. He looks, instead, like someone whose strength is expressed in service, whose authority is exercised in humility, and whose courage is demonstrated not in domination but in vulnerability.

The church does not need more alpha males. It needs more men willing to do what Jesus did: kneel, serve, weep, and absorb the world's violence rather than return it.

The Damage Done

The toxic masculinity movement in the church has caused damage in every direction. It has damaged women, who have been told that their role is to submit, support, and admire — and that resistance to male authority is resistance to God. Women in churches shaped by this theology report feeling invisible, silenced, and instrumentalized — valued for their compliance rather than their gifts, their beauty rather than their wisdom, their willingness to serve male vision rather than their capacity to lead in their own right.

It has damaged men, who have been given a vision of manhood that is impossible to sustain without constant performance and self-suppression. Men who do not fit the alpha-male template — men who are gentle, artistic, emotionally expressive, contemplative — are made to feel that their masculinity is deficient, that they are not the men God designed them to be. The suicide rate among men, the epidemic of male loneliness, the crisis of male emotional illiteracy — these are not unrelated to a cultural and religious framework that tells men their value lies in dominance and their vulnerability is weakness.

It has damaged families, where the theology of male headship has been used to justify patterns of control, emotional abuse, and domestic violence. Not every complementarian household is abusive. But a theology that locates final authority in the husband and frames wifely submission as a divine mandate provides structural cover for abuse when it occurs. The wife who questions her husband's authority can be told she is disobeying God. The husband who controls his wife can frame his control as spiritual leadership. The children who grow up in these households learn that power is gendered, that authority flows in one direction, and that the strongest person in the room is, by definition, the one God has placed in charge.

It has damaged the church's witness. A church that preaches a gospel of sacrificial love while modeling a culture of masculine domination is not merely inconsistent. It is unintelligible. The watching world sees the contradiction even when the church does not. And the watching world draws the obvious conclusion: the church's gospel is not powerful enough to transform its own culture.

Healthy Masculinity in Pastoral Leadership

Healthy masculinity in the pulpit does not require the abandonment of strength, courage, or conviction. It requires the redefinition of these qualities in light of the gospel rather than in light of cultural mythology.

Strength, in the gospel, is the capacity to bear the weight of another's suffering without flinching — not the capacity to impose one's will. Courage is the willingness to be vulnerable, to admit error, to name one's own sin before naming others' — not the willingness to dominate a room. Conviction is fidelity to the truth even when the truth is costly — not the rhetorical force to shout down disagreement.

A pastor who leads with healthy masculinity creates space for others rather than filling it himself. He listens more than he speaks. He asks questions rather than issuing pronouncements. He shares power rather than hoarding it. He admits what he does not know. He models emotional honesty — not the performed vulnerability of the confessional sermon illustration but the genuine, unscripted honesty of a man who has learned that his authority does not depend on his perfection.

He holds his authority lightly, knowing that it belongs to God, not to him. He exercises discipline when necessary — but with grief, not satisfaction. He confronts sin — but his own first. He leads — but toward the cross, not toward the throne.

This is not weakness. It is the hardest kind of strength. The strength to serve rather than dominate. The strength to absorb rather than inflict. The strength to follow a Savior who demonstrated, in the most definitive way possible, that the way up is down, the way to power is through service, and the way to life is through death.

The church that grasps this will not need to manufacture masculine energy or market warrior theology. It will have something far more compelling: men who look like Jesus. And that — not aggression, not domination, not the swagger of the celebrity pastor — is what the world has never seen enough of and has always, whether it knows it or not, been waiting for.

chapters.title: What Is Biblical Justice? Mishpat and Tsedaqah
chapters.summary: Biblical justice is two Hebrew words held together, and the church keeps tearing them apart.
chapters.body:
A widow comes to the gate. The gate is where the elders sit, where the cases are heard, where the field of one man is weighed against the hunger of another. She has no husband to speak for her, no son old enough, no money for the kind of voice that wins. She stands at the edge of the assembly and waits to see whether the word that comes out of that gate will be true. Everything the Bible means by justice is decided in the next ten minutes. Not in the abstract. At the gate. For her.

We have lost the gate. We argue about justice as though it were a theory, a flag, a team. The word has been pulled so far in two directions that for many in the church it now means only one of two things, either a check written to the poor or a vote cast for a party. The Bible's word for justice is older and stranger than both, and it will not fit in either pocket. To recover it we have to learn two Hebrew words and the way they are bound together, because the prophets almost never speak one without the other.

The spine of this whole question is a single verse, and I want to carry it through every turn. 'He has told you, O man, what is good, and what does the Lord require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God' (Micah 6:8 ESV). The word translated justice is mishpat. The word translated kindness, hesed, is the covenant love that keeps faith. And standing behind this verse, woven through Micah's contemporaries, is its partner, tsedaqah. Mishpat and tsedaqah. Justice and righteousness. The prophets pair them so often that to hear one is to expect the other, the way you expect a second footfall after the first. Understand the pair, and you understand what the Bible asks of us at the gate.

Start with mishpat. The simplest definition is the giving of people their due, the rectifying of wrongs, the rendering of a verdict that matches reality. Mishpat is what the elders at the gate are supposed to produce, a judgment that is true regardless of who is standing before them. But the Hebrew is wider than a courtroom. Mishpat includes punishment for the one who wronged the widow, yes, but it also includes care for the widow herself, provision, restitution, the active setting right of what was bent. It is not merely the absence of crime. It is the presence of right outcomes. When Amos thunders 'let justice roll down like waters' (Amos 5:24 ESV), the word is mishpat, and the image is not a trickle of fair verdicts. It is a flood that reaches every dry field, that carries the widow's case all the way downstream to a result she can live on.

Now tsedaqah. We translate it righteousness, and immediately we have shrunk it, because in English righteousness sounds like private virtue, a clean personal record, the moral hygiene of an individual soul. In Hebrew tsedaqah is overwhelmingly relational and social. It means living in right relationship with everyone around you, rendering to each person what the covenant says they are owed, not as a transaction but as a way of being a faithful member of a people. Tim Keller put it well, that tsedaqah is day to day right living and mishpat is rectifying justice, and the Bible welds them so that you cannot have one without the other (Keller 2010). A man could be technically blameless, breaking no law, paying no bribe, and still lack tsedaqah, because tsedaqah asks not merely whether you have done wrong but whether you have done right, whether you have used what you have to repair what is broken near you. Tsedaqah is generous, structural, and active. It is the disposition that produces mishpat as its fruit.

This is the crucial thing the two words do together. Mishpat without tsedaqah becomes mere procedure, a fair trial that no one ever helps the widow reach. Tsedaqah without mishpat becomes private charity, a generous heart that never touches the law that keeps making widows. The Hebrew binds them precisely so that neither can be amputated from the other. And amputation is exactly the church's habit. We keep choosing one word and calling it the whole.

Consider where the pairing shows up. It is not occasional. When God describes the man he chose to found a nation, the reason given is this, that Abraham would command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the Lord by doing righteousness and justice, tsedaqah and mishpat (Genesis 18:19 ESV). The two words are named as the content of the covenant before there is a covenant nation to keep it. When the Psalms describe the throne of God itself, they say righteousness and justice are the foundation of his throne (Psalm 89:14 ESV). The two words are the floor God's own rule stands on. When Isaiah grieves over the failure of Israel, he says God looked for mishpat and behold, bloodshed, for tsedaqah and behold, a cry (Isaiah 5:7 ESV). The two words are what God came looking for and did not find. This is not a marginal theme a few activists have inflated. It is the recurring description of what God is like, what God requires, and what God grieves when it is absent. To miss the pair is to misread the center of the Hebrew Scriptures.

Let me steel-man the first amputation, the one that says justice is fundamentally personal charity. This view is held by serious, faithful people, and it is not selfishness in disguise. Its argument runs deep. Charity, it says, is personal because love is personal. The Good Samaritan did not file a grievance against the Jericho road. He bent down, he bound the wounds, he paid the innkeeper out of his own pocket, he made the suffering of one man his own. The Bible's heroes of mercy are people who give, who sacrifice, who touch. And there is a guarding wisdom here. The moment you make justice a matter of policy alone, you let me off the hook of personal cost. I can vote and stay clean. I never have to bleed the man on the road, never have to know his name, never have to be inconvenienced past the ballot. The charity view is protecting the personal, sacrificial, face to face love that no government program can manufacture. It is protecting hesed, the covenant love standing right there in Micah's verse beside justice. That is real, and a justice that despises it has lost the gospel.

But here is where the strong version of the charity view fails on its own terms. The Good Samaritan is a parable about the man already beaten by the road. It is not a parable about the road. And Scripture also gives us the road. When Isaiah indicts the writers who keep writing oppression, when Amos names those who trample the head of the poor into the dust of the earth and sell the needy for a pair of sandals (Amos 2:6 to 7 ESV), the prophet is not describing a failure of charity. He is describing a market, a court, a structure, working as built. You cannot bind the wounds of a man the system beats faster than you can bandage. Tsedaqah, rightly understood, was never only personal. The covenant itself was structural. Leviticus commands the corners of every field left unharvested for the poor and the stranger, not as charity the farmer chooses but as law the harvest obeys. The Jubilee returned land every fifty years, dissolving accumulated debt by statute, a structural reset written into the constitution of Israel. The sabbath protected the worker and the animal and the foreigner by force of command. These are not charity. These are mishpat built into the architecture of the society, and they are the proof that biblical justice was always meant to touch systems and not merely soothe individuals. The charity view keeps tsedaqah and surrenders mishpat. It has half the verse.

Now steel-man the second amputation, the one that says justice is fundamentally political and structural. This view too is held by the faithful, and it too has deep warrant. It looks at the corners of the field and the Jubilee and says, correctly, that God legislated. God did not leave the poor to the unreliable kindness of the comfortable. He wrote law. He built the protection of the vulnerable into the structure so that it would not depend on whether anyone felt generous that morning. And the structural view sees what private charity is forever tempted to ignore, that a thousand acts of mercy can coexist with an iniquitous decree and never threaten it, that you can run the best soup kitchen in the city and the city will keep producing the hungry faster than you can feed them, because the production of hunger is structural. Abraham Heschel saw this with terrible clarity. The prophet's concern, he wrote, was not with petty wrongs but with the great catastrophe of the whole social order, and the prophet's God was not chiefly a being of metaphysical contemplation but a God of pathos who is personally outraged by injustice (Heschel 1962). The structural view protects the truth that God cares how the society is ordered, not merely how its individuals feel.

But the structural view also fails when it amputates. Make justice only political and you produce a righteousness that can hate. You can crusade for systemic change and despise every actual human being in your path, can want justice for the poor as an abstraction while feeling nothing for the poor man at your own gate, can build a movement that has mishpat as its banner and no hesed in its heart. Micah will not allow it. Do justice, and love kindness, and walk humbly. The same verse. The structural reformer who has lost humility has lost the third clause, and a justice that does not walk humbly with God becomes the libido dominandi wearing a halo, the lust to dominate dressed as liberation. Augustine warned that even the love of justice can be captured by the love of self, that we can crave the position of the one who sets the world right more than we crave the world being right (Augustine 426). The structural view keeps mishpat and risks losing both hesed and humility. It too has half the verse.

So here is the whole verse, and it judges both halves. Mishpat and tsedaqah, justice and righteousness, the rectifying flood and the right daily living that births it, held together, walked out humbly, warmed by hesed. Biblical justice is not charity and it is not politics. It is the restoration of shalom, the woven rightness of all things, and it requires both the bandage and the road, both the Samaritan and the repeal of whatever keeps filling the ditch (Plantinga 1995). The reason the church keeps tearing the two words apart is that each half is cheaper than the whole. The charity half costs my wallet but not my comfort with the system that fills my wallet. The political half costs my vote but not my heart, lets me love humanity while despising my neighbor. The whole costs everything. That is why we avoid it.

There is a history to how we lost this, and it is worth naming with some precision, because the amputation did not happen by accident. For long stretches of the modern Western church, especially after the revivalism of the nineteenth century, the word righteousness was steadily privatized. Tsedaqah, which in Hebrew meant living rightly in the whole web of your relationships and obligations, became in popular preaching a matter of personal piety, the state of an individual soul before God, measured by private morality and private devotion. The social, structural, covenantal weight of the word fell away. By the early twentieth century the split had hardened into a war. The fundamentalist modernist controversy of the 1910s and 1920s forced a choice that the Hebrew never permitted. One side took personal salvation and private righteousness and called the other side worldly. The other side took social reform and structural justice and called the first side escapist. The church divided its own vocabulary down the middle, handed mishpat to one party and tsedaqah to the other, and told each that the other half was a distraction. We are still living in the rubble of that divorce. When a congregation hears the word justice today and immediately files it under politics, or hears the word righteousness and immediately files it under private morality, that reflex is not biblical. It is the inheritance of a hundred year old quarrel that tore one Hebrew pairing into two warring slogans.

Now the reversal, and it lands on the pulpit first, on me. I have preached this verse and stopped at hesed, because hesed preaches warm and mishpat preaches expensive. I have told a congregation to love kindness and walked them right past the word that would have implicated our comfort, our zoning, our quiet arrangements that keep certain widows from certain gates. I did that. The prophets would have named me with the scribes, a writer who keeps writing the comfortable half. Heschel said the prophets were not interested in our religious feelings but in the cry from the gate, and I have too often offered the feelings and muffled the cry (Heschel 1962).

Which brings us, as everything finally does, to the cross, because the cross is where mishpat and tsedaqah meet and refuse to be cheapened. At Golgotha God does mishpat. He does not wave sin away. The bent thing is set right at full cost, the wrong is rectified, the verdict is rendered and the verdict is death. The law is satisfied before grace is spoken, because a justice that simply forgives without rectifying is not mishpat, it is indulgence, and God will not lie about what sin costs. And at the same cross God does tsedaqah. Paul's word for what happens there is the verb form of this very righteousness. God is just and the justifier of the one who has faith (Romans 3:26 ESV). He puts us in right relationship, the relational rightness tsedaqah always meant, by entering the ditch himself, becoming the beaten man on the road, paying the innkeeper with his own blood. The cross is mishpat and tsedaqah in a single body, justice and righteousness welded in the only place they were ever fully joined. Oliver O'Donovan argued that the resurrection vindicates the created moral order, that justice is not our invention to impose but God's order to recover, restored in Christ and entrusted to us as something to receive and not to seize (O'Donovan 1986). Which means I cannot do justice as a conqueror. I can only do it as a man who was himself the beaten one on the road, lifted by a justice I did not earn.

So when the church asks whether justice is charity or politics, the answer is that the question is a trap built to let us keep half. The widow at the gate does not need our theory. She needs mishpat, the verdict that matches reality and the provision that follows it. She needs tsedaqah, a people who live so rightly that her case was repaired before she ever had to plead it. She needs hesed, someone who knows her name. And she needs all three from people who walk humbly, who remember they were once beaten on the same road.

The gate is still there. The widow is still standing at the edge of it. And the word that comes out of that gate is still, somehow, up to us. Let justice roll down. The whole flood. Not half.

### Works Cited

Augustine. 426. The City of God. Translated by Marcus Dods. Edinburgh: T. and T. Clark.

Heschel, Abraham J. 1962. The Prophets. New York: Harper and Row.

Keller, Timothy. 2010. Generous Justice: How God's Grace Makes Us Just. New York: Dutton.

O'Donovan, Oliver. 1986. Resurrection and Moral Order: An Outline for Evangelical Ethics. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Plantinga, Cornelius. 1995. Not the Way It's Supposed to Be: A Breviary of Sin. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

chapters.title: What the Bible Actually Says About Money
chapters.summary: The Bible refuses both the prosperity preacher who blesses your portfolio and the secular reader who reduces it to anti-wealth socialism, and the refusal is the point.
chapters.body:
A man once told me, after a funeral, that he had spent thirty years building something he could not take into the ground he was about to fill. He was not confessing greed. He was confessing surprise. He had played by every rule the culture handed him, and the rules had not lied to him about how to acquire, only about what acquiring would do to him. I have stood at enough gravesides to know that money keeps its promises and breaks them in the same motion. It delivers the house. It does not deliver the man who can live in it.

The question of what the Bible says about money is usually asked by someone who already suspects the answer and wants permission to dislike it. So let me name the real question first, because it is not whether wealth is allowed. The real question is whether money is a neutral tool that takes its moral color from the user, or whether money is a power, an active rival, something that wants you. The Bible answers that second question with a clarity that embarrasses most of our preaching. Money is not neutral. It has a name, and the name is mammon.

The spine of this whole matter runs through one passage, and I want to carry it the entire way. Paul writes to Timothy that godliness with contentment is great gain, that we brought nothing into the world and can take nothing out, and then the sentence everyone misquotes. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. It is through this craving that some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pangs (1 Timothy 6:6-10 ESV). Notice what Paul does not say. He does not say money is the root. He says the love of it is a root, one root among others, and that this love is not a vice on the surface of a life but a craving that reorganizes the whole interior around itself. The word he uses for craving describes a reaching, a stretch toward. Money is not the problem. The stretch is the problem. And the stretch is in me before it is in my bank.

Let me steel-man the two answers that want to silence Paul before he finishes.

The first is the prosperity teaching, and I will not caricature it, because at its best it gets something real. It says God is a Father who gives good gifts, that the creation is good, that poverty is not holy, that the dualism which treats matter as dirty and spirit as clean is a Greek lie the church absorbed and never coughed up. All of that is true. Israel's God made a world of vineyards and oil and wine and called it good before any human ruined it. The Scriptures are full of feasting. Abraham was rich. Job was restored. To pretend the Bible romanticizes destitution is to read it through a monk's bad day. The prosperity preacher is right that God blesses, and right that shame about the body and the field has done real damage. So I take the strongest form of it. God wants to bless His people, and He often blesses them with abundance.

The second answer comes from the other direction, the secular reduction that hears all this talk of the poor and concludes the Bible is simply an ancient socialism, a class document in religious dress, useful for guilt and nothing more. This reading also gets something right. It has actually read the prophets, which is more than many churchgoers can say. It has noticed that Amos thunders against those who sell the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals (Amos 2:6 ESV), that the Jubilee resets debt, that Jesus blesses the poor and warns the rich with a regularity that should unsettle anyone comfortable. The secular reader is right that the Bible is not indifferent to who has and who lacks. It is right that any Christianity which never disturbs the wealthy has not read its own book. So I take the strong form of that too. The Bible is dangerous to the comfortable, and it means to be.

Now watch what Paul's sentence does to both.

The prosperity teaching cannot survive verse nine, where the desire to be rich is itself the trap, where the wanting plunges people into ruin and destruction. Paul is not warning the rich here. He is warning the aspiring, the ones who want to be rich, which is nearly everyone reading this, including the man who writes it. The prosperity gospel takes the legitimate goodness of blessing and bolts a craving onto it, then baptizes the craving. It tells you the stretch is faith. Paul tells you the stretch is a hook. The two cannot both be true.

But the secular reduction cannot survive the passage either, because Paul does not abolish wealth, he disarms it. Three verses later he tells Timothy to command those who are rich, not to stop being rich, but to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share, storing up treasure as a foundation for the future (1 Timothy 6:17-18 ESV). That is not socialism, which seizes. That is not capitalism, which absolves. It is something the modern political menu has no item for. The rich remain rich and are commanded to bleed their wealth outward until it stops being theirs in any way that matters. The Bible does not nationalize the vineyard. It haunts the man who owns it.

So the answer to the real question is neither pole. Money is not morally neutral, which refutes the secular reduction, and money is not safely blessed, which refutes the prosperity preacher. Money is a power, and the only question is who serves whom.

Jesus said it without a single hedge. No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money (Matthew 6:24 ESV). Read it slowly. He does not say you should not. He says you cannot. It is not a prohibition. It is a description of a wiring that will not run two currents. And the word He chooses for money is not the ordinary coin. It is mammon, an Aramaic term He personifies as a rival lord. Jesus is not moralizing about budgets. He is naming a god with a small g and telling you it has applicants for your worship and a contract ready.

This is where the history matters, because the church has known this and forgotten it on a long cycle. In the fourth century, when Constantine's peace flooded the church with wealth it had never held, John Chrysostom preached in Antioch and Constantinople with a ferocity we have lost the stomach for. He told congregations of the newly comfortable that the rich man is a kind of thief, not because he stole, but because what he hoards is the bread of the hungry, the cloak of the naked, the coin owed to the poor (Chrysostom, Homilies on Lazarus). Not to share, Chrysostom said, is to rob. Preaching like that, year after year against the comfort of the powerful, was part of what set the imperial court against him and ended in his exile. We have softened it into a stewardship seminar.

The Reformers wrestled the same beast under the question of usury, the lending of money at interest, which the church had forbidden for over a thousand years on the authority of Scripture. By the sixteenth century commerce had outgrown the prohibition, and Calvin allowed interest within limits, not because he had grown lax but because he distinguished the productive loan from the predatory one. The distinction collapsed almost immediately, as such distinctions do, and within two centuries interest was simply the air the economy breathed. Jacques Ellul, the French theologian and sociologist, watched the end of that long erosion and named what we had done. Money, Ellul argued, is not a tool we picked up but a power we serve, and the modern person's pretense that it is neutral is precisely the lie that lets it rule (Ellul 1984). The man who insists his money is just a tool is the man the tool already owns.

Then came the move that finished us. In 1714, Bernard Mandeville published a poem and then a book, The Fable of the Bees, with the subtitle that should have been a warning, Private Vices, Public Benefits. His argument was simple and corrosive. Greed, vanity, the endless reaching, these private sins are the engine of public prosperity, and a society of saints would be a society of beggars. Adam Smith would later refine the insight into something gentler and truer, but the cultural residue was Mandeville's. We came to believe that the love of money, the very craving Paul called a root of evils, was the secret fuel of the common good. We did not reject Paul's diagnosis. We inverted it. We called the disease the cure.

And once a society decides its central vice is actually its engine, it needs a story about what money is for, a story that quiets the old warnings. Charles Taylor traced how the modern order came to imagine itself as a self-running economic mechanism, a great interlocking exchange in which each person pursuing his own gain produces, as if by design, the good of all (Taylor 2007). It is an elegant picture, and it is not entirely false. Markets do coordinate strangers across distances no charity could reach. But notice what the picture quietly accomplishes. It removes the moral question from the center of economic life and reassigns it to the edges, to private conscience, to what a man does with his surplus on a Sunday. The getting becomes neutral, even virtuous, and only the spending carries any weight. Paul will not allow that division. He locates the danger not in the spending but in the wanting, in the very motion the modern story has declared innocent. The love of money is a root, he says, and roots are underground, in the getting, where we have agreed to stop looking.

Wendell Berry has spent a working life refusing that agreement. He has argued that an economy which treats the love of gain as harmless will inevitably treat everything else, the land, the neighbor, the community, the body, as raw material for that gain, because once the central motion is exempted from judgment there is nothing left to limit it (Berry 1987). Berry writes as a farmer, which matters, because he has watched the abstraction do its work on actual ground, watched the family farm consolidated into the holdings of men who will never see it, watched the field Israel was told not to harvest to its edges reaped now to the very fencerow and beyond. He is describing in modern terms what Isaiah saw in the eighth century before Christ, the joining of house to house and field to field until there is no more room. The machinery is new. The hunger is the same hunger Paul named. It does not change across the millennia. Only its instruments grow more efficient.

And here is the reversal, the place where the objection, followed honestly, turns back toward the cross. The secular reader who says the Bible is just a class document has, without meaning to, paid the gospel a compliment. Because the reader is right that money is about power, right that the having and the lacking are never innocent, right that something is deeply wrong in the distance between the man with the vineyard and the man at his gate. The reader has seen the wound. What the reader has not seen is that the Bible saw it first, named it as sin and not merely as inequality, and refused the two cheap cures the world keeps offering. The world says, seize the vineyard, and calls it justice. The world says, bless the owner, and calls it grace. The gospel says something neither side can stomach. The vineyard owner is a debtor before God, and his only hope is the same as the beggar's.

Press the spine one more time before the cross, because Paul has not finished with us. He says the love of money pierced some through with many pangs, and the verb is worth sitting in. Pierced. Not disappointed, not distracted. Pierced, as a man is pierced who reached for something and was run through by it. This is the testimony of nearly every rich man I have buried and a good many I have counseled while they still had breath. The money did not fail to arrive. It arrived, and it kept arriving, and somewhere in the arriving the man discovered he had been hollowed out to make room for it, that the contentment Paul named at the start of the passage had been the one thing the wealth could not deliver and the one thing he had traded for it. We have all heard the sentiment that money cannot buy happiness, and we file it under platitude. Paul says something far worse. Money can buy the appetite for more money, and that appetite, fed, becomes the whole of a person. The hook does not let go. It sets deeper with every catch.

This is why the cross stands in the center of any honest theology of money, and not as a closing decoration. Gary Anderson has shown that in the biblical and later Jewish imagination, sin was understood as a debt, a weight recorded against the sinner, and that almsgiving to the poor was understood as the paying down of that debt, treasure stored in heaven in the most literal economic grammar (Anderson 2009). When Jesus tells the rich to store up treasure in heaven, He is not speaking in metaphor. He is telling them their accounts are in the wrong bank. And then He does the unthinkable. He pays the debt Himself. He who was rich, Paul says, for our sake became poor, so that we by His poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9 ESV). The richest sentence in the economy of God is a bankruptcy. The Son liquidates everything, down to the garment they gambled for at the foot of the wood, and the liquidation is the inheritance.

This is the law before the grace, and it must come in that order or it is sentiment. The law says the love of money has wormed into every one of us, the prosperity preacher and the prophet of equality alike, and that none of us serves the right master cleanly. The law says I have stretched toward security a thousand times in ways I dressed up as prudence. I have a family. I have five sons. The reaching wears the costume of love and is sometimes only fear. The law indicts the man who writes this before it indicts the man who reads it. Only after that indictment lands does grace mean anything, and then it means everything, because the debt I cannot pay has been paid in a currency I could not have minted.

So what does the Bible actually say about money. It says money is real, good, and dangerous, in that order and all at once. It says the goods of creation are gifts and not garbage, which silences the false holiness of poverty. It says the love of those goods is a root that grows in the dark, which silences the false holiness of wealth. It says you will worship something, and money is the most patient idol you will ever meet, because it never asks for worship in words. It only asks for your trust, a little more each year, until the day a man stands at a graveside and realizes he gave it everything and it gave him a house he is about to leave.

The contentment Paul names is not resignation. It is the freedom of a man who has already been bought, and so cannot be bought again. We brought nothing in. We will take nothing out. Between those two empty hands, the only question worth answering is whose we are. Mammon will take you on any terms. Christ has already paid for you in full. You cannot serve both. You were never able to.

### Works Cited

Anderson, Gary A. Sin: A History. New Haven: Yale University Press, 2009.

Berry, Wendell. Home Economics. New York: North Point Press, 1987.

Ellul, Jacques. Money and Power. Translated by LaVonne Neff. Downers Grove: InterVarsity Press, 1984.

John Chrysostom. On Wealth and Poverty. Translated by Catharine P. Roth. Crestwood: St. Vladimir's Seminary Press, 1984.

Taylor, Charles. A Secular Age. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 2007.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

chapters.title: What the Bible Means by Reconciliation
chapters.summary: We have shrunk a word that once meant the end of a war down to the size of a handshake, and the church is paying for the theft.
chapters.body:
A man stands up after the sermon and says he is tired of the word. Reconciliation, he says, has become a code, a Trojan horse, a way to smuggle a politics into the church under the cover of a Bible word. He is not entirely wrong. The word has been used as cover. But the answer to a stolen word is not to abandon it. The answer is to find out what it meant before we got our hands on it.

The Greek is katallage. It does not come from the language of feelings. It comes from the language of war and the language of money, the exchange that ends a hostility, the settling of an account that stood open between two parties who were enemies. When Paul reaches for it, he is not describing two people deciding to get along. He is describing the end of a conflict that one side could not end on its own.

The spine of this is one passage, and I want to press on it the whole way. All this is from God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of reconciliation, that is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and entrusting to us the message of reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5:18-19 ESV). Read it slowly. God is the actor. We were the enemy. The reconciling happens at the cross, where the trespasses that stood between us and God are not waved away but absorbed, not counted, because they are counted somewhere else, in a body on a tree. Reconciliation in the Bible costs blood. It is never cheap. It is never a feeling.

Now the strongest objection, and it is strong. Some Christians say that this passage is about reconciliation with God and nothing else, that Paul is writing about salvation, about the sinner brought home, and that to extend it to relations between human groups is to bend a vertical text into a horizontal program it was never meant to carry. They say the gospel is reconciliation with God, full stop, and that when we make it about Black and white we have changed the subject from the cross to a cause. I take this seriously because it guards something precious. The vertical is the foundation. A reconciliation between people that is not grounded in reconciliation with God is just diplomacy, and diplomacy does not save.

But read three verses further than we usually stop. The same Paul who wrote 2 Corinthians 5 wrote that Christ is our peace, who has made the two groups one (Ephesians 2:14 ESV), and the two groups he names are not the sinner and God. They are the Jew and the Gentile, two peoples divided by a wall of hostility, made one in the same cross that reconciled them both to God. Paul does not let us choose between the vertical and the horizontal. He fastens them together. The cross that ends the war with God ends the war between us in the same stroke, because the second war was always a symptom of the first. The wall between peoples is held up by the same pride that built the wall between us and heaven.

Willie James Jennings traces how we lost this. In The Christian Imagination he argues that the modern church learned to imagine salvation as the rescue of individual souls from the world, severed from bodies, from land, from peoples, and that this severing was not innocent (Jennings 2010). It happened alongside the colonial enterprise, the very moment European Christians were sorting the peoples of the earth by skin and worth. A faith that could reconcile a soul to God while leaving the slave in the field was a faith that had already cut katallage in half. We kept the vertical and amputated the horizontal, and the amputation was convenient. It let us be saved and stay segregated.

So what does the full word require. First, it requires truth, because you cannot reconcile an account you refuse to read. The reason God could not count our trespasses against us is that he counted them fully, named them, laid them on Christ. There is no reconciliation that skips the naming of the debt. This is where the church most often fails. We want the peace without the ledger. We want the handshake before the truth.
